claim: Software is eating the world, but AI is going to eat software.
assumptions: Deep learning generalizes beyond internet companies to enterprise software
Learned models can replace hand-written code for many functions
predictedOutcome: AI-generated or AI-driven functionality progressively displaces conventional hand-coded software across industries.
contextAtTime: In 2017 deep learning was used at scale mainly by a few internet companies; transformers had just been proposed; few enterprises used ML in production.
outcome: By 2026 AI coding agents and LLM features were pervasive, and fears that AI agents would displace per-seat SaaS triggered a large software-stock selloff in early 2026, though incumbent software revenues kept growing.
verdictRationale: The directional claim, made when AI was marginal in enterprise software, has largely materialized: AI is reshaping how software is built and priced. It was metaphorical rather than precisely testable, so credit is directional.
evolution: Repeated through 2026 in the same form; no revision found.

claim: Accelerated computing and generative AI hit a tipping point; the ~$1 trillion installed base of data centers will in a few years be all accelerated computing, as data centers become 'AI factories'.
assumptions: Generative AI demand persists beyond a hype cycle
CPU performance scaling stays slow
Customers can monetize AI to justify spend
predictedOutcome: Data-center spending shifts decisively from general-purpose CPUs to GPU/accelerated systems over the following few years, with sustained surging demand for NVIDIA.
contextAtTime: NVIDIA data-center revenue had just jumped after ChatGPT; many analysts expected a digestion phase or double-ordering correction in 2024-25.
outcome: Demand kept surging: NVIDIA data-center revenue reached $89.0B in the quarter ended July 2026 (+117% y/y), and hyperscaler capex rose sharply into 2026. CPU servers still exist, so the literal 'all accelerated' has not happened.
verdictRationale: The demand-surge and AI-factory build-out components proved right through mid-2026, against widespread expectations of a correction; the literal claim that the whole installed base becomes accelerated is not yet testable or met.
evolution: Scaled up in 2025 to a $3-4T AI infrastructure forecast by 2030 (see as-huang-8).
audit: [f12] Horizon (2027) is after the cutoff; the literal claim is not yet testable.

claim: Every country needs to own its own AI infrastructure ('sovereign AI'), because AI codifies a nation's culture, intelligence and history; leaders should build the infrastructure as fast as they can.
assumptions: Governments see AI as strategic national infrastructure
Nations will spend public money on domestic compute rather than rely on US hyperscalers
predictedOutcome: Governments and state-linked entities become a major new class of AI-infrastructure buyers.
contextAtTime: Sovereign compute was a niche idea in early 2024; most AI compute was bought by US hyperscalers and labs.
outcome: Through 2025-26 numerous national and Gulf state AI build-outs and 'AI clouds' emerged (recalled; e.g. Saudi, UAE, European initiatives), and NVIDIA's 'AI clouds/industrial/enterprise' customers accounted for a large share of data-center revenue in 2026. Independent quantification of sovereign spend not verified during research.
verdictRationale: The sovereign-AI category clearly materialized as a buyer segment, but its scale relative to hyperscalers could not be independently verified during research; also partly a sales pitch.
evolution: Became a standing theme in NVIDIA keynotes through 2026; no revision found.

claim: If AGI is defined as passing every human test you can imagine, AI will do well on every one within five years; under other definitions AGI may be much further away.
assumptions: Benchmark/test performance continues to scale with compute and data
Test-passing is an adequate operationalization
predictedOutcome: By ~2029 frontier AI passes essentially all human professional and academic exams, including specialized medical boards.
contextAtTime: GPT-4 passed the bar exam but struggled with some specialized medical exams; reasoning models did not yet exist.
outcome: By 2025-26 reasoning models reached gold-medal level on the IMO and high scores on many professional exams, but harder benchmarks remained unsaturated; the horizon has not passed.
verdictRationale: Deadline (2029) not reached; progress is on track for the narrow test-passing definition he explicitly conditioned on.
evolution: No revision found.

claim: It is the job of computing technology to make it so nobody has to program; the programming language is human, so children should focus on domain expertise rather than learning to code.
assumptions: LLMs become reliable enough to translate natural language into working software
Domain expertise becomes the scarce skill
predictedOutcome: Natural-language programming becomes mainstream and reduces the need for most people to learn conventional programming.
contextAtTime: GitHub Copilot autocompletion was common, but autonomous coding agents were not yet usable; most experts still advised learning to code.
outcome: By 2025-26 natural-language 'vibe coding' and coding agents were mainstream (e.g. over a quarter of new Google code AI-generated by late 2024; agent tools triggering a 2026 SaaS selloff), but professional programming did not disappear.
verdictRationale: Direction (natural language as the programming interface) proved right faster than most expected; the stronger implication that people need not learn programming is not established.
evolution: No revision found.

claim: Reasoning models can consume 100 times more compute, and future reasoning models will consume much more compute; DeepSeek R1 is an excellent innovation that increases, not decreases, demand.
assumptions: Test-time compute scaling keeps improving model quality
Cheaper reasoning expands usage faster than per-query efficiency falls
predictedOutcome: Despite efficiency gains like DeepSeek's, aggregate demand for NVIDIA compute keeps rising strongly.
contextAtTime: DeepSeek's low reported training costs had just triggered a ~17% one-day NVIDIA selloff and fears of a compute glut.
outcome: NVIDIA revenue more than doubled year over year to $96.2B in the quarter ended July 2026, with data-center revenue up 117%; hyperscalers raised capex sharply.
verdictRationale: Made against the prevailing market fear, the claim that reasoning and efficiency would expand compute demand was borne out by 2026 demand data. Interested party, but the outcome is independent.
evolution: Reinforced at GTC 2025/2026; no revision found.

claim: US export controls on AI chips to China were a failure: they cut NVIDIA's China share from ~95% to ~50% and motivated and accelerated Chinese competitors; later, 'China is going to win the AI race' (walked back to 'nanoseconds behind').
assumptions: Chinese domestic chips (e.g. Huawei Ascend) can substitute adequately
Beijing will favor domestic suppliers when US chips are restricted
predictedOutcome: Continued controls would cost NVIDIA the Chinese market and strengthen Chinese chip and AI ecosystems rather than slow them.
contextAtTime: H20 sales had just been restricted ($5.5B charge); DeepSeek had shown Chinese labs could compete on constrained hardware. Anthropic and others argued for tighter controls.
outcome: By 2026 NVIDIA's China data-center sales were near zero: even after the US licensed H200 sales, Beijing withheld approval to foster domestic suppliers, sales were under 1% of data-center revenue, and NVIDIA guided to no China data-center revenue.
verdictRationale: His prediction that NVIDIA would lose China and that China would push domestic substitutes was borne out; whether controls 'failed' at slowing Chinese AI, and whether China 'wins', remain contested and unresolved.
evolution: Shifted from '95% to 50%' (May 2025) to '95% to zero' (Oct 2025) to 'China will win' then 'nanoseconds behind' (Nov 2025), and in May 2026 'the market will open over time'.
audit: [f30] Bundles statements from May, Oct and Nov 2025 under one date; the May 2025 statement is the dated claim, later remarks are context.

claim: AI infrastructure spending will reach $3 trillion to $4 trillion by the end of the decade.
assumptions: AI revenues grow enough to justify capex
Power and supply-chain constraints are overcome
No sharp financing pullback
predictedOutcome: Annual AI infrastructure spend of roughly $3-4T by ~2030.
contextAtTime: Huang cited ~$600B in 2025 hyperscaler data-center capex; bubble concerns were widespread.
outcome: Spending kept climbing into 2026 (e.g. Microsoft quarterly capex ~$41B, Alphabet and Meta guiding roughly to doubled 2026 capex), but the 2030 target is years away.
verdictRationale: Deadline not reached; 2026 capex is on an upward trajectory consistent with but far from proving the forecast.
evolution: Reiterated after the Nov 2025 earnings; no revision found.

claim: NVIDIA has roughly $500 billion of Blackwell and Rubin demand visibility through calendar 2026 (raised at GTC 2026 to ~$1 trillion through 2027); there is no AI bubble.
assumptions: Customer commitments convert to shipments
Financing for AI labs and neoclouds holds up
predictedOutcome: Blackwell+Rubin revenue of ~$500B over 2025-2026.
horizon: through calendar 2026 (and 2027 for the raised figure)
contextAtTime: Analysts questioned the figure (part already shipped; trued-up backlog ~$307B); AI-bubble talk peaked in late 2025.
outcome: By the quarter ended July 2026 NVIDIA was reporting $96.2B quarterly revenue and guiding $108B for the next quarter, consistent with the trajectory; calendar 2026 is not complete.
verdictRationale: The window (end-2026) has not closed; run-rate through mid-2026 is consistent with the claim, but the total cannot yet be checked.
evolution: Raised to ~$1T through 2027 at GTC 2026.

claim: Bots are the new apps; human language is the new UI ('conversation as a platform').
assumptions: NLP becomes good enough for open-ended conversation
Users prefer conversational interfaces to apps for many tasks
predictedOutcome: Conversational agents replace a large share of app interactions.
contextAtTime: Pre-transformer NLP; the 2016 chatbot wave (Messenger bots, Cortana, Microsoft's Tay failing the same week) was brittle.
outcome: The 2016 bot wave fizzled, but LLM-based chat (ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini) made conversation a mass-market interface from 2023, with agents spreading in 2025-26.
verdictRationale: The thesis was right but the 2016 technology could not deliver it; it came true only after LLMs, roughly seven years later.
evolution: Revived in 2023 as 'copilots' and in 2024-25 as agents (see as-nadella-5).

claim: Invest $1B in OpenAI and become its exclusive cloud, jointly building Azure AI supercomputers aimed at AGI (followed by ~$10B in 2023).
assumptions: Scaling large models on massive compute will produce commercially valuable capabilities
Exclusive cloud access confers platform advantage
predictedOutcome: OpenAI models become a major driver of Azure and Microsoft product revenue.
contextAtTime: GPT-2 had just been released; scaling laws were not yet published; most of big tech did not back an outside lab at this scale.
outcome: Microsoft's stake in OpenAI Group PBC was valued at ~$135B (~27%) in Oct 2025, OpenAI committed an incremental $250B to Azure, and Azure passed $100B annual revenue in FY2026.
verdictRationale: A contrarian bet made before scaling laws were established, it generated large strategic and financial returns by 2025-26.
evolution: Hedged in 2024 (Suleyman's Microsoft AI) and restructured in Oct 2025 (non-exclusive compute, expert-panel AGI test).

claim: With the AI-powered Bing, Microsoft would challenge Google, 'the 800-pound gorilla' in search: 'I want people to know that we made them dance.'
assumptions: Chat-based answers erode Google's search advantage
Early access to GPT-4 confers a lasting product lead
predictedOutcome: Bing gains meaningful search/AI-assistant share from Google.
contextAtTime: ChatGPT had reached ~100M users; Google appeared caught flat-footed and Bard's demo had a factual error.
outcome: Google did respond (Bard, AI Overviews, Gemini), but by 2026 Gemini was outpacing Microsoft's consumer Copilot and Google's search franchise remained dominant.
verdictRationale: The literal claim (forcing Google to react) came true, but the implied market-share shift in search did not occur.
evolution: No public revision found; Microsoft's consumer focus shifted to Copilot under Suleyman.

claim: Copilots will be the new UI for knowledge work; Microsoft 365 Copilot priced at $30 per user per month for enterprises.
assumptions: Enterprises see enough productivity ROI to pay a large per-seat premium
Model quality sufficient for everyday Office tasks
predictedOutcome: Rapid, broad paid adoption of Microsoft 365 Copilot across the commercial seat base.
contextAtTime: Generative AI enthusiasm was peaking; ROI evidence for enterprise copilots did not yet exist.
outcome: Microsoft 365 Copilot reached ~30M paid seats by mid-2026 (per a low-reliability report), a small fraction of Microsoft's several-hundred-million commercial Office seats, after a slow 2024 ramp.
verdictRationale: Adoption became material by 2026 but far slower and narrower than the 'every knowledge worker' framing implied.
evolution: Messaging shifted in 2024-25 from copilots to agents.

claim: Business applications are essentially CRUD databases with business logic; in the agent era that logic will migrate to AI agents and SaaS business apps as we know them will collapse.
assumptions: Agents become reliable enough to operate across systems of record
Value shifts to an 'AI tier' above databases
predictedOutcome: Per-seat SaaS business apps lose value to agent layers; vendors restructure around agents.
contextAtTime: Agents were early and unreliable; SaaS revenues were growing normally.
outcome: In Feb-Mar 2026 software stocks sold off sharply on exactly this fear (SEG SaaS Index -25.7% YTD at March 31), though software earnings were still growing and some recovery followed.
verdictRationale: Markets priced the thesis in 2026, but no actual collapse of SaaS revenues had occurred by October 2026; open-ended.
evolution: No revision found.

claim: Jevons paradox strikes again: as AI gets more efficient and accessible, its use will skyrocket, turning it into a commodity we just can't get enough of.
assumptions: Demand for AI is highly price-elastic
Efficiency gains (e.g. DeepSeek) lower prices rather than just margins
predictedOutcome: Cheaper AI increases total compute and cloud demand rather than shrinking it.
contextAtTime: DeepSeek R1 had just triggered fears that cheaper models would shrink demand for GPUs and data centers.
outcome: Azure grew ~40%+ into 2026 and passed $100B annual revenue; NVIDIA data-center revenue more than doubled y/y; hyperscaler capex rose.
verdictRationale: Made in the middle of a market panic, the claim that efficiency would expand demand was borne out by 2026 usage and capex data.
evolution: Microsoft briefly slowed some data-center leases in early 2025, then resumed heavy capex; no revision of the view found.

claim: Self-claiming some AGI milestone is nonsensical benchmark hacking; the real benchmark is whether the world economy grows at ~10% (developed world ~7%).
assumptions: Transformative AI would show up in productivity and GDP statistics
predictedOutcome: AGI should not be declared until macro growth visibly accelerates.
contextAtTime: OpenAI's contract with Microsoft let OpenAI's board declare AGI, which would cut off Microsoft's IP rights; labs were touting benchmark wins.
outcome: No acceleration of global growth toward 10% was evident by 2026; in Oct 2025 the renegotiated deal required any AGI declaration to be verified by an independent expert panel.
verdictRationale: This is a criterion rather than a forecast; it was reflected in the 2025 contract, but whether AI eventually drives such growth is unresolved.
evolution: Became part of the Oct 2025 contract (expert-panel AGI verification).

claim: The binding constraint on AI build-out is no longer chip supply but power and ready data-center shells; otherwise chips end up 'sitting in inventory that I can't plug in'.
assumptions: Grid interconnection and construction lag GPU supply
predictedOutcome: Power availability, not GPUs, limits hyperscaler AI capacity growth in 2026.
contextAtTime: GPU supply had loosened relative to 2023-24; utilities and grid queues were becoming the bottleneck; Zuckerberg had made a similar argument in 2024.
outcome: Microsoft kept capex at record levels into 2026 (~$41B in the June 2026 quarter); no independent 2026 source on power-limited deployments was gathered during research.
verdictRationale: Plausible and widely echoed, but not independently verified with 2026 outcome data in during research.
evolution: No revision found.

claim: Over time, the computer itself, whatever its form factor, will be an intelligent assistant helping you through your day; we will move from mobile first to an AI first world.
assumptions: Machine learning keeps improving across speech, vision and language
Assistants become the primary interface
predictedOutcome: AI assistants become a primary computing interface and Google reorients around AI.
contextAtTime: Weeks after AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol; voice assistants were narrow; transformers did not yet exist.
outcome: By 2025-26 general AI assistants (Gemini, ChatGPT, Copilot) were mass-market, and Gemini was gaining against Copilot; Google's whole stack had reoriented around AI.
verdictRationale: An early, clear strategic forecast that materialized, though Google was not first to deliver the breakthrough assistant (OpenAI was).
evolution: Reaffirmed repeatedly; no revision found.

claim: AI is one of the most important things humanity is working on; more profound than, I dunno, electricity or fire — but like fire, its downsides must be overcome.
assumptions: AI becomes a general-purpose technology with economy-wide effects
predictedOutcome: AI's long-run impact exceeds that of electricity.
contextAtTime: Before transformers were widely used; AI mainly in recommendation, search and perception.
outcome: AI became the dominant technology investment theme of 2023-26, but its civilizational significance relative to electricity is not yet assessable.
verdictRationale: Not falsifiable on a 2026 horizon.
evolution: Repeated on 60 Minutes in 2023; no revision found.

claim: Launch Bard and bring generative AI into Google Search, ending Google's cautious slow-release posture.
assumptions: Search's moat survives the shift to AI answers if Google integrates them itself
Google's models can catch up to OpenAI
predictedOutcome: Google defends search leadership by integrating generative AI rather than being displaced by chatbots.
contextAtTime: ChatGPT's success and Microsoft's Bing launch led many to predict the decline of Google search; Google reportedly declared a 'code red'.
outcome: Google shipped AI Overviews (2024), AI Mode and Gemini; by 2026 Gemini was outpacing Microsoft's Copilot and Google remained the dominant search provider, while publishers reported traffic losses.
verdictRationale: The defensive integration strategy succeeded in preserving Google's position through 2026, though it came after OpenAI had seized first-mover advantage.
evolution: Accelerated with Gemini (Dec 2023) and AI Overviews (May 2024).

claim: The risk of underinvesting is dramatically greater than the risk of overinvesting in AI infrastructure; even if over-invested, the infrastructure is widely useful to Google.
assumptions: AI is a platform shift where losing position is costlier than excess capacity
Excess capacity can be redeployed internally
predictedOutcome: Alphabet keeps raising AI capex despite ROI questions.
contextAtTime: Analysts were beginning to question AI capex returns (e.g. Sequoia's '$600B question', summer 2024).
outcome: Alphabet capex rose to ~$91B in 2025 and was guided to roughly $175-185B for 2026 (recalled); Pichai himself warned of 'elements of irrationality' in Nov 2025. Whether the spend earns adequate returns is not yet known.
verdictRationale: A risk judgement whose payoff depends on long-run AI returns that cannot yet be measured.
evolution: Paired in Nov 2025 with an acknowledgment of bubble-like irrationality (see as-pichai-7).

claim: I think the progress is going to get harder. When I look at 2025, the low-hanging fruit is gone; the hill is steeper (though there is no definitive wall).
assumptions: Pretraining scaling returns are diminishing
New breakthroughs needed for further gains
predictedOutcome: Visible AI capability gains in 2025 slow relative to 2023-24.
contextAtTime: Reports that OpenAI's next model showed smaller gains; Altman said 'there is no wall'; o1-style reasoning had just appeared.
outcome: Pretraining-only gains did slow, but 2025 brought large capability jumps via reasoning/RL and test-time compute (e.g. IMO gold-level results, Gemini 2.5 and Gemini 3) and surging compute demand.
verdictRationale: Right that easy pretraining gains were exhausted, but wrong if read as a slowdown in overall 2025 progress, which accelerated via new techniques, including at Google.
evolution: By mid-2025 he described current systems as 'AJI' with rapid progress expected through 2030.

claim: We are in an era of 'artificial jagged intelligence' (AJI); AI will make dramatic progress by 2030 but full AGI will likely arrive somewhat after 2030.
assumptions: Uneven capabilities persist and require further breakthroughs to fix
predictedOutcome: No broadly accepted AGI before ~2030; large capability advances before then.
contextAtTime: Peers (Altman, Amodei) were giving 2026-2028 timelines; Hassabis said 5-10 years.
outcome: No consensus AGI by October 2026.
verdictRationale: Horizon not reached.
evolution: No revision found.

claim: The AI investment boom is both rational and has elements of irrationality; if the bubble bursts, no company is going to be immune, including Google.
assumptions: Investment is outpacing near-term revenue
A correction would propagate across the ecosystem
predictedOutcome: A possible correction in AI investment that would hit all players, while long-run impact remains profound.
contextAtTime: Late-2025 bubble debate after circular deals among OpenAI, NVIDIA, Oracle and AMD.
outcome: Through Oct 2026 no broad AI investment collapse occurred; capex and NVIDIA revenue kept rising, while AI-exposed software stocks did see a sharp 2026 selloff.
verdictRationale: A conditional warning whose condition (a burst) had not occurred by the cutoff.
evolution: Coexists with his 2024 'underinvesting is the bigger risk' stance.

claim: Create a dedicated fundamental AI research lab (FAIR) led by Yann LeCun.
assumptions: Deep learning will be core to Facebook's products
Open research attracts top talent
predictedOutcome: Facebook becomes a leading AI research organization.
contextAtTime: One year after AlexNet; Google had acquired DNNresearch (Hinton); deep learning was not yet mainstream in industry.
outcome: FAIR produced PyTorch and the Llama models, but its influence waned after 2025 reorganization into Meta Superintelligence Labs and LeCun's departure in Nov 2025.
verdictRationale: An early bet on deep learning that produced foundational tools (PyTorch) and the Llama line.
evolution: FAIR deprioritized relative to MSL in 2025.

claim: Within the next decade, the metaverse will reach a billion people, host hundreds of billions of dollars of digital commerce and support jobs for millions of creators and developers.
assumptions: VR/AR hardware becomes mass-market
Social presence in 3D drives engagement
predictedOutcome: ~1B metaverse users by ~2031.
contextAtTime: Pandemic-era enthusiasm for virtual worlds; generative AI was not yet mainstream.
outcome: Reality Labs accumulated >$70B in operating losses; metaverse budgets were reportedly cut by up to ~30% in late 2025 as resources moved to AI and AI glasses (recalled).
verdictRationale: Deadline (2031) not reached, though the trend through 2026 is strongly against the forecast.
evolution: De-emphasized from 2023 in favor of AI (see reversal).

claim: Meta's long-term vision is to build general intelligence and open source it responsibly; Meta will have ~350,000 H100s (~600,000 H100-equivalents) by end of 2024.
assumptions: Scaling compute yields general intelligence
Open release is compatible with safety and Meta's business
predictedOutcome: Meta becomes a frontier lab releasing open models toward AGI.
contextAtTime: Llama 2 was the leading open model; Meta had pivoted from the metaverse a year earlier.
outcome: Meta built the compute, but its open frontier strategy faltered after Llama 4 (2025); it reorganized under Meta Superintelligence Labs and signaled more selective open-sourcing.
verdictRationale: An aspiration; AGI not reached and the open-source component was partly abandoned.
evolution: Recast in 2025 as 'personal superintelligence' with selective open-sourcing.

claim: Energy, not chips, will become the binding constraint on scaling AI: gigawatt-scale data centers take years of permitting and power build-out.
assumptions: Demand for training/inference compute keeps growing exponentially
Grid expansion is slow and regulated
predictedOutcome: Power availability becomes the main bottleneck for AI data centers within a few years.
contextAtTime: In early 2024 GPU supply was still the widely cited bottleneck.
outcome: By late 2025 Microsoft's CEO said its constraint was power and data-center shells rather than chips, and gigawatt-scale campuses became the norm.
verdictRationale: He identified power as the next bottleneck when chips were the consensus constraint; an independent peer confirmed it by late 2025. Outcome evidence is a single interested party, so confidence is moderate.
evolution: Meta later announced gigawatt-scale campuses (Prometheus, Hyperion) consistent with this view (recalled).
audit: [f11] Power-not-chips: graded partial and on-time for consistency with as-asch-5 — chips, HBM and packaging also bound through 2026.

claim: Open source AI is the path forward: like Linux, open models will become the industry standard, and starting next year Meta expects future Llama models to become the most advanced in the industry.
assumptions: Open ecosystems out-iterate closed labs
Meta can sustain frontier training and still release weights
predictedOutcome: Llama models lead the industry from 2025 and open models become the standard.
contextAtTime: Llama 3.1 405B had just closed much of the gap with GPT-4o; DeepSeek and Qwen were rising but less visible in the West.
outcome: Llama 4 (April 2025) did not lead and drew criticism; the strongest open-weight models of 2025 came from Chinese labs; Meta formed MSL and signaled it would be careful about open-sourcing frontier models. Open weights did spread (even OpenAI released gpt-oss).
verdictRationale: The specific, dated forecast that Llama would be the most advanced in 2025 failed; the broader open-weights trend was partly right but led by others.
evolution: Walked back in the July 2025 'Personal Superintelligence' letter (selective open-sourcing).
audit: Two parts: 'open source becomes the standard' (not borne out at the frontier) and 'Llama most advanced in 2025' (did not happen). Verdict incorrect on the testable part.
interpretations: Open weights did come within months of the frontier (DeepSeek, Qwen).
But Llama did not lead, and Meta itself retreated from open frontier releases in 2026.

claim: In 2025, Meta and other companies will have an AI that can effectively be a sort of mid-level engineer writing code.
assumptions: Coding agents become reliable on real codebases within a year
predictedOutcome: During 2025 AI agents do substantial mid-level engineering work at Meta.
contextAtTime: Coding assistants were strong at autocomplete; autonomous agents (Devin etc.) were unreliable.
outcome: Coding agents improved dramatically in 2025 and drove a 2026 SaaS selloff, but no public evidence was found that Meta's agents functioned as mid-level engineers in 2025.
verdictRationale: Capability trend was right in direction, but the specific claim of mid-level-engineer equivalence in 2025 was not demonstrated.
evolution: No revision found.

claim: Form Meta Superintelligence Labs, invest ~$14.3B in Scale AI and hire top researchers at extreme pay because developing superintelligence is now in sight; aim for 'personal superintelligence' while being careful about what to open source.
assumptions: Superintelligence is achievable within a few years with sufficient talent and compute
Talent concentration can close Meta's frontier gap
predictedOutcome: Meta returns to the frontier with superintelligence-class models within a few years.
contextAtTime: Llama 4 had disappointed; OpenAI, Google and Anthropic led; peers gave 2026-2030 AGI timelines.
outcome: Meta continued heavy spending (2026 capex guided ~$115-135B, recalled); LeCun left in Nov 2025. Status of MSL frontier models by Oct 2026 could not be verified during research.
verdictRationale: Outcome of the superintelligence push is not yet assessable.
evolution: Marks a reversal from the 2024 open-source stance.

claim: If Meta ends up misspending a couple of hundred billion dollars that would be unfortunate, but the risk is higher on the other side: being out of position if superintelligence arrives sooner.
assumptions: The payoff from leading in superintelligence dwarfs capex losses
Meta's ad cash flows can absorb overspending
predictedOutcome: Meta keeps escalating capex despite bubble risk.
contextAtTime: Late-2025 AI bubble debate; Meta raising capex and taking on off-balance-sheet data-center financing.
outcome: Meta guided 2026 capex to roughly $115-135B (recalled); returns not yet assessable.
verdictRationale: A risk judgment whose outcome depends on future AI returns.
evolution: Consistent with Pichai's 2024 underinvestment argument; no revision found.

claim: High-Flyer acquired ~10,000 Nvidia A100 GPUs (by 2021) for its Fire-Flyer clusters before US export controls, a compute base later used for DeepSeek.
assumptions: Large-scale compute would be strategically valuable and scarce
predictedOutcome: Owning a large GPU cluster becomes a decisive advantage for Chinese AI work.
contextAtTime: In 2021 few Chinese firms outside big tech bought GPUs at this scale; export controls on A100s came in Oct 2022.
outcome: US controls (Oct 2022 onward) cut off A100/H100-class sales; DeepSeek used its stockpile and H800s to train V3/R1, becoming China's leading open model lab.
verdictRationale: The pre-control stockpile proved strategically decisive; however the action was made for quant trading, so the 'belief' about LLMs is partly retrospective.
evolution: No revision found.
audit: [f16] The A100 purchase was completed by ~2021 for quant trading; redated and originality lowered — its LLM rationale is partly retrospective.

claim: DeepSeek will pursue AGI through fundamental research rather than near-term applications or commercialization, without seeking outside financing.
assumptions: High-Flyer profits can fund frontier research
A small, young, research-driven team can compete with big tech
predictedOutcome: DeepSeek becomes a research-first frontier lab rather than an application company.
contextAtTime: Chinese 'hundred-model war' after ChatGPT; most startups raised VC and chased applications.
outcome: DeepSeek released V2, V3 and R1 as research-led open models with novel efficiency techniques and remained largely focused on models rather than consumer monetization; AGI not achieved.
verdictRationale: The organizational aspiration was carried out, but its stated goal (AGI) is unresolved.
evolution: No revision found.

claim: In the face of disruptive technologies, moats created by closed source are temporary; even OpenAI's closed-source approach cannot prevent others from catching up. A team's culture and talent are the real moat.
assumptions: Algorithmic efficiency and open publication diffuse capabilities quickly
Compute gaps can be partly offset by efficiency
predictedOutcome: Open models (including DeepSeek's) catch up to closed frontier models, eroding closed-source advantages.
contextAtTime: OpenAI's GPT-4o led; Llama 3 was the leading open model; DeepSeek was known mainly for cheap V2 pricing.
outcome: DeepSeek-V3 (reported ~$5.6M final training run) and R1 (MIT license) approached o1-level reasoning, triggering a ~17% NVIDIA one-day drop; OpenAI later released open-weight gpt-oss models and its Microsoft deal was revised to allow open weights.
verdictRationale: Within six months DeepSeek itself demonstrated that closed leads were narrow, and closed labs moved toward open weights; frontier leadership nonetheless stayed with closed US labs.
evolution: No revision found.

claim: China's AI cannot remain a follower; Chinese firms must contribute original innovation rather than free-ride. Money is not DeepSeek's problem; the embargo on high-end chips is.
assumptions: Chinese researchers can produce frontier-level original work
Compute restrictions are the binding constraint
predictedOutcome: Chinese labs move from imitation to original contributions while chip access limits scale.
contextAtTime: Western consensus held that Chinese labs lagged 1-2 years and mostly followed US innovations.
outcome: DeepSeek's MLA/MoE efficiency methods and GRPO-based reasoning were widely adopted; Chinese labs led open-weight models in 2025. Huang called China 'nanoseconds behind'. Chip constraints persisted: NVIDIA's China sales stayed near zero in 2026 amid US and Chinese restrictions.
verdictRationale: Chinese original innovation and the chip bottleneck were both borne out, though overall frontier leadership remained with US labs.
evolution: No revision found.

claim: Price DeepSeek-V2's API near cost (far below rivals), reflecting architecture-driven cost reductions rather than a deliberate price war.
assumptions: MoE + latent-attention efficiency sharply lowers serving cost
Cheap access grows the user/developer base
predictedOutcome: Inference prices collapse and efficiency becomes a competitive axis.
contextAtTime: Chinese LLM APIs were priced near Western levels; efficiency was not the main competitive narrative.
outcome: Major Chinese providers (ByteDance, Alibaba, Baidu) cut prices within weeks (recalled), and DeepSeek's efficiency later reset global expectations about training and inference costs.
verdictRationale: The pricing move precipitated a price war and showcased efficiency gains that reshaped the market in 2025.
evolution: No revision found.

claim: Restructured OpenAI from a nonprofit into a capped-profit entity and took Microsoft's $1B investment, betting that AGI requires capital and compute at a scale philanthropy cannot supply.
assumptions: Capability keeps scaling with compute
Products funded by frontier models can generate revenue to finance more compute
predictedOutcome: OpenAI would need, and be able to raise, multi-billion-dollar capital through commercial products and a hyperscaler partner.
contextAtTime: In 2019, GPT-2 had just been released; the scaling-laws paper was not yet published, and few labs spent at this scale.
outcome: OpenAI raised far larger sums (Microsoft about $13B; Stargate), reported an annualized revenue run rate of about $50B to $70B by Sep 2026, and recapitalized as a public benefit corporation in Oct 2025.
verdictRationale: The implied belief that frontier AI is capital-intensive and commercially fundable was borne out, and early. In 2019 it was a minority bet; profitability and governance costs remain unresolved.
evolution: Extended through the Oct 2025 recapitalization and about $1.4T of compute commitments.

claim: In the next five years, computer programs that can think will read legal documents and give medical advice.
assumptions: Language-model capability keeps improving with scale
Users and institutions are willing to rely on AI for professional-domain tasks
predictedOutcome: By about 2026, AI systems routinely read legal documents and give medical advice.
contextAtTime: GPT-3 (2020) was impressive but unreliable; few experts expected mainstream professional use within five years.
outcome: By 2023 to 2026, LLM assistants were widely used to review legal documents and answer medical questions. Professional-standard autonomous advice without human oversight was not established, and 'can think' remains contested.
verdictRationale: The surface behavior (reading legal documents, giving medical advice) was widely achieved within the window, starting with GPT-4 in 2023, which was bold for 2021. Trackers disagree only on whether advice meets a professional standard.
evolution: No revision found; later essays (2024 to 2025) generalized it into broader AGI and superintelligence claims.

claim: If AI-driven wealth is taxed through company equity and land (an 'American Equity Fund'), it could pay every US adult about $13,500 a year within 10 years. AI will shift wealth from labor to capital.
assumptions: AI drives very rapid GDP and asset growth
Political adoption of new wealth taxes
predictedOutcome: By about 2031, AI-generated wealth could fund about $13,500 per adult per year if the proposed taxes were adopted.
contextAtTime: A 2021 pre-ChatGPT policy essay; UBI was a niche topic.
outcome: No such fund exists. AI has concentrated value in a few companies, and general goods (housing, healthcare, education) have not followed a 'Moore's Law' decline. The horizon has not been reached.
verdictRationale: This is conditional on a policy that was not adopted, and the 2031 horizon has not passed.
evolution: Altman later floated 'universal basic compute' ideas (2024, recalled) instead of the equity-fund design.

claim: Proposed that the US (or a global body) license AI models above a capability threshold, with testing requirements and independent audits, and a regulator able to revoke licenses.
assumptions: Capability thresholds can be defined and measured
A regulator can keep pace with frontier labs
predictedOutcome: A licensing regime for frontier models would reduce catastrophic risk without stopping progress.
contextAtTime: Six months after ChatGPT, there was bipartisan appetite for AI regulation, and Gary Marcus testified alongside him in favor of licensing. Critics saw regulatory-capture motives.
outcome: No US federal licensing agency was created. The 2023 executive order's reporting rules were rescinded in Jan 2025, and Altman later argued against pre-approval regimes (recalled).
verdictRationale: A normative policy proposal, not a forecast. It was not adopted, and its merits cannot be falsified.
evolution: Softened by 2025: he favored light-touch federal rules and warned against pre-approval (recalled, ev-altman-17).

claim: It is possible that we will have superintelligence in 'a few thousand days (!); it may take longer, but I'm confident we'll get there.'
assumptions: Deep learning keeps scaling predictably
Sufficient compute and energy are built
predictedOutcome: Superintelligence within roughly 5 to 15 years of Sep 2024 (a few thousand days), hedged as 'possible'.
horizon: a few thousand days from Sep 2024 (about 2030 to 2035)
contextAtTime: o1 reasoning models had just been previewed. Pretraining returns were being debated, and many researchers (LeCun, Marcus) disputed near-term superintelligence.
outcome: As of Oct 2026, no system was broadly recognized as superintelligent, though frontier models showed expert-level performance in narrow domains (competition math, coding).
verdictRationale: The horizon has not been reached, and the claim was hedged as 'possible'.
evolution: Reinforced in Reflections (Jan 2025) and The Gentle Singularity (Jun 2025), which said 'we are past the event horizon'.

claim: In 2025, we may see the first AI agents 'join the workforce' and materially change the output of companies.
assumptions: Agent reliability is good enough for unsupervised multi-step work
Enterprises integrate agents into workflows within a year
predictedOutcome: During 2025, some companies deploy AI agents that materially change their output.
contextAtTime: Agents (Operator, early coding agents) were demos at the start of 2025, and reliability on long tasks was poor.
outcome: Coding agents (Codex, Claude Code, Cursor agents) were widely adopted in 2025. McKinsey found 62% of firms experimenting with agents but no more than 10% scaling them in any function, and only 39% reporting any enterprise EBIT impact from AI. Karpathy called 2025 the start of a 'decade of agents'.
verdictRationale: The hedged 'may see the first' was met in software engineering, where agents materially changed output at some firms. Broad workforce integration with measured output change had not happened by end-2025.
evolution: In The Gentle Singularity (Jun 2025) he said 2025 had seen agents doing real cognitive work, especially code.
interpretations: Coding agents did change output at many firms in 2025 — partially right.
General-purpose 'digital employees' did not join the workforce in 2025.

claim: The cost to use a given level of AI falls about 10x every 12 months, and lower prices lead to much more use.
assumptions: Algorithmic efficiency, distillation and hardware improvements continue
Demand is highly price-elastic (Jevons effect)
predictedOutcome: The price for a fixed capability level keeps falling about 10x per year, and total usage and spend rise.
contextAtTime: He cited the roughly 150x drop in per-token price from GPT-4 (early 2023) to GPT-4o (mid-2024), and DeepSeek-V3 and R1 had just shown cheap near-frontier models.
outcome: Per-token prices for fixed capability kept falling steeply through 2025 to 2026 (GPT-5 family, gpt-oss, Chinese open-weight models). Total spend rose sharply: OpenAI run rate went from above $20B at end-2025 to a reported $50B to $70B in Sep 2026.
verdictRationale: Both halves (rapid price decline per capability and rising total usage) were consistent with the data available. The exact 10x rate varies by capability threshold.
evolution: No revision found.

claim: 2026 will likely see the arrival of systems that can figure out novel insights.
assumptions: Reasoning and RL scaling keeps improving
Novel insights can be verified (math proofs, experiments)
predictedOutcome: During 2026, AI systems produce verifiably new scientific or mathematical results.
contextAtTime: Scientists were sceptical (TechCrunch). Reasoning models had shown competition-level math but no accepted original research results.
outcome: By early 2026, GPT-5.2 models were credited in Terence Tao's Erdős-problems database with complete solutions to problems #205 and #652, with no prior literature found. A Nov 2025 OpenAI paper collected cases of GPT-5 contributing new research steps. A walked-back Oct 2025 claim shows the evidence needs care.
verdictRationale: Verifiable, modest novel math results arrived in the predicted window. The significance of the insights is debated and the year is not over, so this is provisional.
evolution: No revision found; the 2027 robotics step of the same schedule is unresolved.
audit: 'Novel insights in 2026' verdict rests on contested reports of model-assisted math results; confidence lowered.

claim: Committed OpenAI to about 30 GW of compute (about $1.4T over roughly 8 years) and set an aspiration to add 1 GW of compute per week.
assumptions: Demand for AI keeps growing fast enough to service the commitments
Capital markets keep financing at high valuations
Scaling compute keeps yielding more valuable models
predictedOutcome: Revenue grows into hundreds of billions to justify the commitments, and capacity is built on schedule.
contextAtTime: OpenAI was about to exceed $20B annualized revenue (end-2025). Analysts questioned financing, and some (for example David Cahn's '$600B question') had flagged an AI capex-revenue gap.
outcome: By Sep 2026, OpenAI's reported run rate was about $50B (Bloomberg) to nearly $70B (Axios), and it was reportedly raising at least $30B at about a $1.4T valuation. The commitments are mostly still ahead.
verdictRationale: This is a multi-year bet. Revenue has grown fast, but nowhere near the scale needed to cover $1.4T, so it is not yet judgeable.
evolution: Escalated from the $500B Stargate announcement (Jan 2025).

claim: Language-model performance improves as a smooth power law in model size, data and compute. Scaling these up (the 'big blob of compute') is the main driver of capability.
assumptions: Power laws continue beyond the measured range
Enough data and compute can be obtained
predictedOutcome: Larger models trained with more compute will be predictably more capable, which justifies orders-of-magnitude compute increases.
contextAtTime: In 2020 most of the field doubted that scale alone would yield general capabilities; GPT-3 had not yet been released.
outcome: Scaling drove GPT-3, GPT-4, Claude and Gemini capability gains through 2024. From 2024 to 2025, gains increasingly came from RL and inference-time scaling as well as pretraining, and pretraining returns were debated.
verdictRationale: A contrarian, empirically grounded bet that defined the industry's strategy for five years. It was refined, not refuted, by later reasoning-scaling.
evolution: From 2024 to 2025 he extended the thesis to RL and test-time compute.

claim: Co-founded Anthropic: a safety-focused lab must itself build frontier models to do relevant safety research and set norms (a 'race to the top').
assumptions: Safety research needs frontier-scale models
A safety brand can be commercially competitive
predictedOutcome: Anthropic stays at the frontier while influencing industry safety norms.
contextAtTime: OpenAI had just signed with Microsoft; there were few independent frontier labs.
outcome: Claude models were among the frontier leaders, especially in coding. Anthropic's run rate was reported at about $19B in early 2026. Responsible-scaling-style policies were adopted by other labs.
verdictRationale: The commercial viability of a safety-branded frontier lab was demonstrated. Whether it actually improved safety outcomes is not measurable.
evolution: Accepted Gulf sovereign investment (2025, recalled) and pushed the frontier, so critics saw convergence with competitors.

claim: A model that, over an hour of conversation, seems like a generally well-educated human could be two or three years away.
assumptions: Continued scaling of pretraining and post-training
predictedOutcome: By about 2025 to 2026, conversational models are indistinguishable from an educated human in casual hour-long conversation.
contextAtTime: GPT-4 and Claude 2 were fluent but error-prone. Most forecasters placed robust human-level conversation further out.
outcome: By 2025, frontier models (GPT-4.5, Claude 3.7/4, Gemini 2.5) were judged human in controlled Turing-test studies (recalled: a 2025 UCSD study found GPT-4.5 judged human more often than humans) and were widely used as general assistants. Agentic economic autonomy, which he did not claim, remained limited.
verdictRationale: The narrow, explicitly scoped claim (conversational generalist) was met within the window. He explicitly did not claim economic transformation.
evolution: Upgraded to the 'powerful AI as early as 2026' claim (Oct 2024).

claim: 'Powerful AI' (smarter than Nobel laureates across most fields, a 'country of geniuses in a datacenter') could come as early as 2026, though it could take much longer.
assumptions: Scaling of pretraining and RL continues
Autonomous long-horizon task ability emerges
Enough compute is available
predictedOutcome: Earliest case: systems meeting his powerful-AI definition exist in 2026, with a central expectation around 2026 to 2027.
horizon: as early as 2026; possibly much longer
contextAtTime: Claude 3.5 Sonnet and o1-preview had just been released, and AI scientific discovery was not yet demonstrated.
outcome: As of Oct 2026, no system was widely accepted as meeting the powerful-AI definition (Nobel-level across fields, autonomous multi-week work). Models produced modest novel math results and strong coding agents.
verdictRationale: 'As early as 2026' was the optimistic edge of a hedged range. The central window (2026 to 2027) is not over, but the earliest case looks unlikely to be met in 2026.
evolution: Repeated through 2025, with talk of 2026 to 2027 at Davos 2025 (recalled), and in the Jan 2026 essay (recalled, low confidence).

claim: DeepSeek-V3's low training cost was roughly on the expected cost-reduction curve, not a unique breakthrough. Strict US chip export controls are decisive for keeping a US-led (unipolar) AI world around 2026 to 2027.
assumptions: Compute remains the binding constraint for frontier AI
Export controls can be enforced against smuggling
predictedOutcome: With tight controls, Chinese labs stay behind the frontier; without them, they reach parity.
contextAtTime: DeepSeek R1 had triggered a market selloff and a narrative that cheap training made compute less important. Nvidia (Huang) opposed controls.
outcome: Compute demand did not collapse, and hyperscaler capex rose. US policy shifted toward allowing some Nvidia sales to China (H20 in 2025 and later H200, recalled), while Chinese open-weight models stayed close behind the frontier.
verdictRationale: His cost-curve reading of DeepSeek fit the evidence and the compute-demand collapse narrative proved wrong. The policy counterfactual (controls being decisive) cannot be tested because the controls were loosened.
evolution: Continued advocacy into 2025 to 2026; a public clash with Huang (Jun 2025).
audit: [f13] Core claim (export controls decisive for a unipolar world ~2026–27) not yet testable.

claim: In three to six months AI will be writing 90% of the code, and in 12 months we may be in a world where AI writes essentially all of the code.
assumptions: Coding agents improve rapidly
Developers adopt agentic tools at scale
Code volume, not human design work, is what is measured
predictedOutcome: By about Sep 2025, 90% of new code is AI-written; by about Mar 2026, nearly all.
contextAtTime: Claude 3.7 Sonnet and early Claude Code were just out. Google said about 25% of its new code was AI-generated (Oct 2024).
outcome: At Anthropic itself, leaders reported roughly 70 to 90% of code written by Claude by late 2025. Industry-wide shares were lower: Microsoft about 20 to 30% (Apr 2025) and Google at least 25 to 30%. 'Essentially all code' was not reached industry-wide by Mar 2026.
verdictRationale: The directional bet (rapid shift to AI-written code) was right, and it came true inside frontier labs. As a general claim on his stated timeline, it overshot.
evolution: Later framed as true 'at Anthropic' and in some teams (recalled), narrowing the scope.
audit: [f10] Industry-wide share of AI-written code was far below 90% within 3–6 months (lab-internal shares were high). Graded incorrect for consistency with other direction-right, magnitude/timing-wrong dated claims (khosla-2, hinton-2, musk-8).
interpretations: Inside frontier labs and AI-native startups, ~90% AI-written code was reported by 2025–26.
Industry-wide, the share was far lower within the 3–6 month window — the claim overreached in scope.

claim: AI could wipe out half of all entry-level white-collar jobs and push unemployment to 10 to 20% within the next one to five years.
assumptions: Agents become reliable for routine knowledge work
Firms substitute rather than augment
Policy does not offset displacement
predictedOutcome: By 2026 to 2030, a large decline in entry-level white-collar employment and US unemployment of 10 to 20%.
contextAtTime: Unemployment was about 4%. Anecdotal reports of hiring freezes for juniors existed but there was little hard data. Huang publicly rejected the warning.
outcome: Early signals: a Stanford study (Aug 2025) found a 13% relative employment decline for 22-to-25-year-olds in the most AI-exposed occupations. The Yale Budget Lab (Oct 2025) found no broad occupational disruption. Aggregate US unemployment stayed far below 10% through the data available (2026 labor data not verified during research).
verdictRationale: The window runs to 2030 and was framed as 'could'. Early entry-level effects are consistent in direction, but the aggregate unemployment component shows no sign yet.
evolution: He repeated the warning through 2025 and proposed measures such as a 'token tax' (recalled).

claim: Goal: by 2027 interpretability should be able to reliably detect most model problems (an 'MRI for AI'). This is a race against capabilities that may reach a 'country of geniuses' first.
assumptions: Mechanistic interpretability scales to frontier models
Labs invest enough
predictedOutcome: By 2027, interpretability tools can reliably diagnose most model problems.
contextAtTime: Anthropic had published dictionary-learning features (2024) and circuit tracing (2025), and interpretability was still far from diagnostic use.
outcome: Interpretability research progressed, and Anthropic reported using it in pre-deployment audits (recalled). No field-wide reliable diagnostic exists as of Oct 2026.
verdictRationale: This is a self-set goal with a 2027 deadline.
evolution: No revision found.

claim: Kept Anthropic's usage limits barring Claude's use for mass domestic surveillance and fully autonomous weapons, even at the cost of a confrontation with the US Department of Defense.
assumptions: Usage restrictions are enforceable and matter for safety
Commercial and political costs are survivable
predictedOutcome: Anthropic keeps its restrictions despite losing some government business.
contextAtTime: Frontier labs were competing for national-security contracts (about $200M each in 2025, recalled).
outcome: Recalled: the administration ordered agencies off Anthropic and labelled it a supply-chain risk, and Anthropic contested this. The final status as of Oct 2026 was not verified.
verdictRationale: A values-driven action whose consequences were still playing out, and the facts could not be verified during research.
evolution: Consistent with the 2025 'Urgency of Interpretability' and earlier safety commitments.

claim: DeepMind's mission: solve intelligence, then use it to solve everything else, via general-purpose learning systems inspired by neuroscience and reinforcement learning.
assumptions: General learning algorithms exist and can be found
Large resources (Google) are available
predictedOutcome: General AI that then accelerates science across domains.
contextAtTime: Deep learning was newly practical (AlexNet 2012, DQN 2013), and AGI as a stated corporate goal was fringe.
outcome: DeepMind delivered AlphaGo, AlphaFold (Nobel 2024) and Gemini. 'Solve intelligence' remains unachieved, and the general path that worked was transformer scaling rather than the RL-first approach.
verdictRationale: An open-ended mission statement. The science-acceleration half is partly vindicated.
evolution: Kept the mission, but adopted LLM scaling (Gemini) as the main path after 2023.

claim: Deep neural networks combined with tree search and self-play reinforcement learning can master Go, a domain considered intractable for brute-force search.
assumptions: Learned value and policy functions generalize across Go positions
predictedOutcome: AlphaGo beats top professionals years ahead of expert expectations.
contextAtTime: Experts commonly estimated superhuman Go was about a decade away.
outcome: AlphaGo beat Fan Hui (2015) and Lee Sedol 4-1 (Mar 2016). AlphaZero generalized the approach (2017), and search plus learned evaluation influenced later reasoning-model research.
verdictRationale: Achieved well ahead of consensus expectations at the time.
evolution: No revision found.
audit: [f2] Same AlphaGo result as as-silver-1; counted once and as track record, not foresight.

claim: AI can solve fundamental scientific problems such as protein structure prediction and become a primary tool for scientific discovery.
assumptions: Rich structured datasets (PDB) and strong inductive biases
Problem has clear evaluation (CASP)
predictedOutcome: AI achieves near-experimental accuracy on protein folding and is adopted by biologists.
contextAtTime: Protein folding had been an unsolved 50-year challenge, and CASP progress was incremental before AlphaFold 1 (2018).
outcome: AlphaFold 2 reached near-experimental accuracy at CASP14, released over 200M structures, and earned Hassabis and Jumper the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
verdictRationale: Demonstrated and independently recognized by the Nobel committee.
evolution: Extended to drug discovery (Isomorphic) and AlphaFold 3 (2024).
audit: [f4] Dated at the CASP14 result it is credited with predicting; treated as track record. 'Primary tool for scientific discovery' is too vague for specificity 4.

claim: AI risk should be treated as seriously as the climate crisis, with an IPCC-like scientific body and CERN- or IAEA-like international institutions. Extinction risk should be a global priority.
assumptions: International coordination is feasible
Risks are serious enough to justify oversight
predictedOutcome: Creation of international scientific and oversight institutions for frontier AI.
contextAtTime: Ahead of the Bletchley AI Safety Summit, shortly after the CAIS statement.
outcome: National AI safety institutes and an International AI Safety Report (chaired by Bengio, 2025) emerged. No binding IAEA-like body exists, and US policy shifted toward deregulation in 2025.
verdictRationale: A normative proposal, only partially institutionalized.
evolution: Continued to call for international standards in 2025 (recalled).

claim: The billions flowing into generative-AI startups bring crypto-like hype and some grifting. AI is overhyped in the short term but underhyped in the long term.
assumptions: Valuations are running ahead of near-term product value
predictedOutcome: Some AI startup valuations will deflate, while long-run impact exceeds expectations.
contextAtTime: Early 2024 saw a funding boom for LLM wrappers and model startups.
outcome: Several 2023-vintage model startups were absorbed (Inflection into Microsoft, Character.ai into a Google license, Adept into Amazon), while frontier-lab valuations and capex kept rising through Oct 2026 with no broad crash.
verdictRationale: Partly borne out for second-tier startups. The overall hype claim is not falsifiable yet.
evolution: Repeated the bubble-in-parts framing in 2025 (recalled).

claim: Expects the first AI-designed drugs from Isomorphic Labs to be in clinical trials by the end of 2025.
assumptions: AI-designed candidates pass preclinical work
Regulatory filings proceed on schedule
predictedOutcome: At least one Isomorphic AI-designed drug enters human clinical trials by Dec 2025.
contextAtTime: Several other AI-discovered molecules (for example Insilico's) were already in trials, and Isomorphic had partnerships with Lilly and Novartis.
outcome: Not verified during research. To the analyst's recall, Isomorphic said in mid-2025 it was preparing for first human trials, and no public first-dosing announcement by end-2025 was confirmed.
verdictRationale: The horizon passed, but the outcome could not be verified. If no trial started in 2025, the verdict would be 'incorrect' (late).
evolution: Not tracked.
audit: [f1] Deadline (end-2025) passed with no public first-dosing announcement recorded by the cutoff, so resolved as incorrect (low confidence: flips if a 2025 trial start is documented).

claim: AGI, meaning a system with all the cognitive capabilities of humans, could arrive within the next 5 to 10 years.
assumptions: Scaling plus one or two further breakthroughs
Continued investment
predictedOutcome: AGI by about 2030 to 2035.
contextAtTime: Altman and Amodei gave 2026-to-2027 timelines and LeCun and Marcus decades. Hassabis positioned himself in the middle.
outcome: Not reached by Oct 2026; the horizon is open.
verdictRationale: The horizon has not been reached.
evolution: Shortened modestly from 'within a decade' (2023) to '5 to 10 years' (2025), and has been stable since.

claim: Scaling is necessary but probably not sufficient for AGI. One or two more breakthroughs may be needed, such as world models, planning, continual learning and fixing 'jagged' inconsistency.
assumptions: Current LLM paradigm has structural gaps
predictedOutcome: Progress will require architectural additions (for example Genie-style world models), not just larger LLMs.
contextAtTime: There was a 2024 to 2025 debate on pretraining returns. LeCun argued LLMs are a dead end, while Altman and Amodei stressed scaling.
outcome: Google DeepMind invested in world models (Genie 3, Aug 2025, recalled) alongside Gemini scaling. Inconsistency ('jaggedness') remains a recognized limitation as of 2026.
verdictRationale: A view about future necessity that is not yet testable.
evolution: Consistent through 2025; disputed LeCun's 'no general intelligence' claim in Dec 2025 (recalled).

claim: Merged DeepMind and Google Brain into Google DeepMind under his leadership to build Gemini, a frontier general model competing directly with OpenAI.
assumptions: Google's compute (TPUs), data and distribution can be turned into frontier products quickly
predictedOutcome: Google regains frontier leadership in general models.
contextAtTime: Google was seen as having fallen behind after ChatGPT (the Bard launch stumble, Feb 2023).
outcome: Gemini 2.5 (2025) and Gemini 3 (late 2025, recalled) were at or near the top of major benchmarks, and Gemini Deep Think won IMO 2025 gold.
verdictRationale: Google DeepMind reached frontier parity or leadership within about two years, consistent with the bet.
evolution: No revision found.

claim: AI is probably humanity's biggest existential threat; with artificial intelligence 'we are summoning the demon'. Regulatory oversight is needed.
assumptions: Superhuman AI is achievable and hard to control
predictedOutcome: Advanced AI poses extinction-level risk unless regulated.
contextAtTime: In 2014, Bostrom's Superintelligence had just been published, and mainstream ML researchers largely dismissed existential risk.
outcome: Existential-risk concern became mainstream (CAIS statement 2023, with Hinton and Bengio). Musk himself built frontier AI (xAI) from 2023.
verdictRationale: An unfalsifiable risk opinion, though early relative to the mainstream.
evolution: He kept the rhetoric (for example a 10 to 20% chance AI 'goes bad', recalled) while founding xAI.

claim: Co-founded and funded OpenAI as a nonprofit, open counterweight to Google/DeepMind's concentration of AI talent.
assumptions: A nonprofit can attract talent and compute to rival Google
Openness reduces risk
predictedOutcome: OpenAI becomes a leading lab that remains nonprofit and open.
contextAtTime: DeepMind was the dominant AGI lab after Google acquired it in 2014.
outcome: OpenAI became the leading commercial lab but moved to capped-profit (2019) and a public benefit corporation (2025), with mostly closed frontier weights. Musk left the board in 2018 and sued in 2024.
verdictRationale: It did become a counterweight to Google, but the nonprofit and open structure the action assumed did not survive frontier capital needs.
evolution: Reversed into litigation (2024) and a takeover bid (2025).

claim: Tesla will demonstrate a fully autonomous drive from Los Angeles to New York, with no one touching the controls, by the end of 2017.
assumptions: Camera-based neural nets plus fleet data quickly solve driving edge cases
predictedOutcome: A coast-to-coast autonomous demo by Dec 2017.
contextAtTime: Waymo and others were years into testing, and most experts considered L4/L5 highway-to-city driving years away.
outcome: No such demonstration took place in 2017 or for years after.
verdictRationale: A specific, dated deadline that was missed, and contrary to expert consensus at the time.
evolution: The deadline rolled forward annually in later statements.

claim: Tesla will have over a million robotaxis on the road next year (2020), subject to regulatory approval.
assumptions: FSD software reaches driverless reliability via over-the-air updates
Regulators approve
predictedOutcome: About 1M Tesla vehicles operate as driverless robotaxis in 2020.
contextAtTime: Tesla's FSD was driver-assist (L2), and Waymo operated a small supervised service.
outcome: No Tesla robotaxis operated in 2020. A limited pilot with safety monitors launched in Austin only in June 2025.
verdictRationale: Off by more than five years and by orders of magnitude in fleet size. The regulatory caveat does not explain a technology that was not ready.
evolution: Restated with new dates repeatedly (2020 to 2025).

claim: OpenAI breached its founding commitment to develop AGI as an open-source nonprofit for humanity and became a closed de facto Microsoft subsidiary. He sued and released Grok-1's weights two weeks later.
assumptions: A binding founding agreement existed
Open weights serve safety and the public interest
predictedOutcome: Courts constrain OpenAI's for-profit conversion; open models gain legitimacy.
contextAtTime: OpenAI and Microsoft were dominant. OpenAI published Musk's emails showing he had supported a for-profit path in 2017 to 2018.
outcome: OpenAI completed its recapitalization into a public benefit corporation under nonprofit control (Oct 2025) and released gpt-oss open weights (Aug 2025). The trial outcome as of Oct 2026 was not verified during research.
verdictRationale: The legal outcome was not verified. The open-weights pressure he advocated was partly reflected in OpenAI's 2025 release.
evolution: Escalated with the $97.4B takeover bid (Feb 2025).

claim: If AGI means smarter than the smartest human, it will probably arrive next year (2025), within two years.
assumptions: Compute and power constraints are overcome quickly
Scaling continues
predictedOutcome: A system smarter than the smartest human at most tasks by 2025 or 2026.
contextAtTime: GPT-4-class models were strong but far below top-human performance in research, planning and reliability.
outcome: By Oct 2026, models reached top-human level in narrow competitions (IMO gold, Jul 2025) but were not generally smarter than the smartest humans, and no consensus AGI existed.
verdictRationale: The two-year window (to about April 2026) passed without broadly superhuman general AI, which was the claim's own definition.
evolution: He kept pushing the date out (for example AGI in 2026, smarter than all humans combined by about 2030; recalled).

claim: Built xAI's Colossus 100k-GPU cluster in 122 days and pledged to double it, betting that raw compute scale is the decisive input for frontier AI.
assumptions: Compute scale translates into model leadership
Capital and power can be secured quickly
predictedOutcome: xAI reaches the frontier quickly via compute.
contextAtTime: xAI was a year old, and Grok-1 and Grok-2 trailed GPT-4o and Claude 3.5.
outcome: Grok 3 (Feb 2025) and Grok 4 (Jul 2025) reached or approached frontier benchmark levels (recalled). xAI's commercial share remained small relative to OpenAI and Anthropic.
verdictRationale: Compute scale bought benchmark parity quickly, but not market leadership.
evolution: Scaled further toward gigawatt-class Colossus 2 (recalled).

claim: Tesla would build on the order of several thousand Optimus humanoid robots in 2025 to do useful work in its factories.
assumptions: Hardware (hands, actuators) is production-ready
AI policies generalize to factory tasks
predictedOutcome: Thousands of Optimus units doing useful work in Tesla factories by end-2025.
contextAtTime: Optimus demos were partly teleoperated (Oct 2024 'We, Robot' event), and humanoid production at scale was unproven industry-wide.
outcome: Reports through 2025 indicated production far below the thousands targeted, with redesigns delaying volume.
verdictRationale: The specific annual volume target was missed, according to the available (recalled) reporting.
evolution: Volume targets were pushed to 2026 and later (recalled).

claim: Tesla's autonomous ride-hailing would cover roughly half of the US population by the end of 2025, pending regulatory approvals.
assumptions: Rapid regulatory approvals across states
Unsupervised FSD reliability
predictedOutcome: Robotaxi service areas covering about half the US population by Dec 2025.
contextAtTime: The Austin pilot had just launched (June 2025) with safety monitors in a geofenced area, while Waymo operated in a handful of metros.
outcome: By end-2025, Tesla operated limited services in Austin and the Bay Area (the latter with safety drivers), far from half the US population.
verdictRationale: The coverage target was missed by a wide margin. The regulatory caveat does not account for a gap of this size.
evolution: Continues his pattern of annual robotaxi deadlines.

claim: LLM hallucinations will be largely eliminated by around 2025, as models learn to know when they don't know.
assumptions: Calibration and retrieval techniques mature quickly
predictedOutcome: Hallucination ceases to be a material problem in frontier models by about 2025.
contextAtTime: Hallucination was the top enterprise complaint about GPT-4-era models.
outcome: Hallucination rates fell on some benchmarks, but the problem persisted: OpenAI's Sep 2025 paper treats it as ongoing, and o3 and o4-mini showed higher hallucination rates than o1 on PersonQA (Apr 2025).
verdictRationale: The problem was not 'largely eliminated' by 2025, and reasoning models in some cases increased it.
evolution: No explicit revision found.

claim: Proposed a 'modern Turing test' for 'artificial capable intelligence': an AI that, given $100,000, autonomously turns it into $1 million. He suggested such ACI could arrive within the next few years.
assumptions: Agents gain planning, tool use and long-horizon autonomy
They can transact in the real economy
predictedOutcome: An AI passes the $100k-to-$1M test within about two years (about 2025).
contextAtTime: Autonomous agent demos such as AutoGPT (2023) were unreliable.
outcome: No verified case of an AI autonomously turning $100k into $1M. Anthropic's Project Vend (Jun 2025) showed a Claude-run shop losing money.
verdictRationale: Nothing passed the test by 2025. The exact timing in the original wording is uncertain, so confidence is low.
evolution: Later framed autonomy as something to limit ('humanist superintelligence', 2025).

claim: The 'containment problem': AI (with synthetic biology) will proliferate in ways that make containment look impossible, yet containment must be made possible through safety engineering, audits, chokepoints such as chips, and international alliances.
assumptions: Capabilities diffuse rapidly
States can coordinate on chokepoints
predictedOutcome: Without deliberate containment, powerful capabilities diffuse widely and quickly.
contextAtTime: The book appeared in Sep 2023, before open-weight frontier-near models (Llama 3, DeepSeek) were widespread.
outcome: Capabilities diffused fast: near-frontier open-weight models from China (DeepSeek, Qwen) and the US (gpt-oss) arrived by 2025. Chip export controls were used but then loosened (recalled).
verdictRationale: The diffusion premise was borne out, while the normative containment agenda has not been realized. Overall it is not falsifiable.
evolution: In 2025 he reframed the goal as 'humanist superintelligence' and limits on autonomy.

claim: Within about five years, everyone will have their own AI personal assistant or 'chief of staff' that knows them and acts for them (the Pi thesis).
assumptions: Personal AI with memory and agency becomes reliable and trusted
predictedOutcome: Mass adoption of personalized AI assistants by about 2028.
contextAtTime: Pi had launched (May 2023) and ChatGPT was the only mass-market assistant.
outcome: By 2026, general assistants (ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, Meta AI) had hundreds of millions of users and were adding memory and agent features. Pi itself did not achieve scale.
verdictRationale: The horizon has not been reached. The trajectory supports the adoption half, but not via his own company.
evolution: Carried into Microsoft Copilot's 'AI companion' positioning (2024 to 2025).

claim: Left Inflection's independent path to lead Microsoft AI, implying that frontier and consumer AI require hyperscaler-scale capital and distribution.
assumptions: Independent model startups cannot match hyperscaler compute and distribution
predictedOutcome: Independent second-tier model startups consolidate into big tech.
contextAtTime: Inflection had raised $1.3B in 2023 but Pi lagged ChatGPT, and the cost of a frontier training run was escalating.
outcome: Similar acqui-hire and licensing deals followed: Adept and Amazon (Jun 2024), Character.ai and Google (Aug 2024) (recalled). Only a few independent labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI) stayed at the frontier, each with enormous capital.
verdictRationale: The consolidation pattern implied by the move happened promptly.
evolution: In 2025 he pushed Microsoft toward its own frontier models (MAI) and superintelligence team.

claim: 'Seemingly conscious AI' could be built within 2 to 3 years with existing techniques. Labs should not build AI that presents as a person or claims consciousness, and AI welfare and rights research is premature and dangerous ('psychosis risk').
assumptions: Memory, personality and agency features combine into a convincing persona
Users anthropomorphize strongly
predictedOutcome: By about 2027 to 2028, widely deployed AI that many users believe is conscious, with social and legal pressure for AI rights.
contextAtTime: Reports of 'AI psychosis' and teen-harm lawsuits had appeared, and Anthropic had begun model-welfare research (2025).
outcome: As of Oct 2026, companion-AI attachment and safety concerns were active policy issues (recalled), and no consensus or legal recognition of AI consciousness existed.
verdictRationale: The horizon has not been reached.
evolution: Developed further in his 'humanist superintelligence' framing (Nov 2025).

claim: Launched Microsoft AI's superintelligence team to pursue 'humanist superintelligence': domain-specific, controllable, superhuman systems (for example medical) rather than unbounded autonomous AGI.
assumptions: Domain-bounded superintelligence is achievable and safer
Microsoft can build frontier models independently of OpenAI
predictedOutcome: Microsoft fields its own frontier-class models and domain superhuman systems.
contextAtTime: The Oct 2025 Microsoft-OpenAI restructuring had just freed Microsoft to pursue AGI on its own, and MAI-1-preview had been released (Aug 2025, recalled).
outcome: Not verified for 2026 during research.
verdictRationale: An early-stage strategic program.
evolution: New in 2025.

claim: Most professional white-collar tasks done at a computer (for example accounting, legal and project management) will be fully automated by AI within the next 12 to 18 months.
assumptions: Agents become reliable enough for end-to-end professional tasks
Enterprises deploy quickly
predictedOutcome: By roughly mid-2027 to late 2027, most such tasks are fully automated.
contextAtTime: Coding agents were mature, while the broader enterprise agent rollout was limited (McKinsey 2025).
outcome: The horizon has not been reached.
verdictRationale: The deadline is after 2026-10-11. The source attribution itself is low confidence.
evolution: Escalation from his 2023 ACI framing.

claim: Large deep convolutional networks trained on GPUs with lots of labelled data can decisively beat hand-engineered computer vision (AlexNet, with Krizhevsky and Sutskever).
assumptions: GPU compute and ImageNet-scale data suffice to make deep nets outperform feature engineering
predictedOutcome: Deep neural networks become the dominant approach in vision and then other perception tasks.
contextAtTime: Neural nets were a minority approach in 2012 computer vision; SVMs and hand-crafted features dominated.
outcome: AlexNet won ILSVRC-2012 by a wide margin; deep learning became the dominant paradigm across AI and underpins all frontier models through 2026.
verdictRationale: The bet on large GPU-trained neural nets was contrarian in 2012 and was decisively vindicated.
evolution: Hinton's group was acquired by Google (DNNresearch, 2013); no revision of the core view.
audit: [f2] AlexNet is the authors' own demonstrated result — foundational, but not a forecast.

claim: People should stop training radiologists now; it is completely obvious that within five years deep learning will do better than radiologists — it might be ten years.
assumptions: Image classification accuracy translates into replacing the radiologist's job
Regulation, liability and workflow would not slow substitution
Radiologists' work is mostly image reading
predictedOutcome: By ~2021 (at most ~2026) deep learning outperforms radiologists enough that training new radiologists is unnecessary.
contextAtTime: Deep CNNs had just surpassed humans on ImageNet classification (2015); early papers showed strong results on specific medical imaging tasks.
outcome: By 2025-26 the US and UK faced radiologist shortages; US average radiologist pay rose to ~$571k in 2025 (+9% y/y, Medscape) and case loads rose ~25% 2018-early 2025. AI tools are used as aids, not replacements; Mayo Clinic's radiology staff grew ~55% since 2016.
verdictRationale: The 5-year horizon (Nov 2021) passed with AI used as an aid, not a replacement; the explicit advice to stop training radiologists was refuted by rising radiologist demand. The 10-year hedge ends Nov 2026, just after the cutoff, with no sign of displacement.
evolution: Reported to have later acknowledged he was off the mark (only weak LinkedIn-level evidence seen; NYT/Fortune revisited the claim in 2025-26). His 2025 job-loss warnings shifted to 'mundane intellectual labor' broadly.
audit: [f15] The 5-year horizon (Nov 2021) passed with AI used as an aid, not a replacement, and the advice to stop training radiologists was refuted by rising radiologist demand and pay. The 'might be ten years' hedge runs to Nov 2026, just after the cutoff; Hinton later said he was too early and too specific.
interpretations: Strict reading: radiologists were not outperformed or displaced within 5 or 10 years — incorrect.
Charitable reading: AI does outperform radiologists on narrow detection tasks; the error was assuming task performance implies job loss.

claim: He was 'deeply suspicious' of back-propagation: 'My view is throw it all away and start again.'
assumptions: Brain-like (largely unsupervised) learning requires a mechanism other than backprop
Further progress needs a new learning algorithm
predictedOutcome: Progress toward more general AI would require replacing backprop-based training.
contextAtTime: Backprop-trained deep nets were dominant; Hinton was pursuing capsule networks (2017) and brain-inspired alternatives.
outcome: All frontier systems 2017-2026 (transformers, LLMs, reasoning models) remain backprop/gradient-descent trained; alternatives such as capsules and forward-forward have not displaced it.
verdictRationale: The subsequent decade of progress came entirely from scaling backprop-trained transformers; Hinton himself reversed in 2023, arguing backprop may be superior to the brain's learning.
evolution: Reversed by May 2023: concluded digital nets with backprop may learn better than biological brains, which became a basis for his risk concerns.
