claim: Left Google to speak freely about AI dangers; revised his estimate for AI smarter than humans from '30 to 50 years or even longer away' to roughly 5 to 20 years.
assumptions: Capabilities of LLMs like GPT-4 continue to scale
Digital learning (weight sharing across copies, backprop) is more efficient than biological learning
predictedOutcome: AI broadly smarter than humans arrives roughly between 2028 and 2043.
contextAtTime: ChatGPT (Nov 2022) and GPT-4 (Mar 2023) had just shown rapid capability gains; the FLI pause letter had been published in March 2023.
outcome: As of Oct 2026 no consensus that AI is smarter than humans across the board; Hinton himself shortened the estimate further in 2025.
verdictRationale: Horizon extends to 2043; earliest bound (2028) not yet reached.
evolution: Shortened again by April 2025 to 'a good chance it'll be here in 10 years or less'.

claim: Estimated a 10% to 20% chance that AI leads to human extinction within about the next 30 years ('Not particularly, 10% to 20%' when asked if he had revised it).
assumptions: Superintelligent AI is built
Control/alignment is not solved
Competitive dynamics prevent a halt
predictedOutcome: A 10-20% probability of AI-caused human extinction or takeover over ~30 years.
contextAtTime: Made weeks after his Nobel Prize in Physics (Oct 2024); frontier labs racing on reasoning models.
outcome: No resolution possible as of Oct 2026; he repeated a 'sort of 10 to 20% chance' of AI taking control in April 2025.
verdictRationale: Probabilistic, long-horizon claim; not falsifiable by 2026.
evolution: Earlier cited ~10%; raised range to 10-20% and has kept it through 2025.

claim: On AI surpassing humans in every domain: 'there's a good chance it'll be here in 10 years or less.'
assumptions: Agentic AI and continued scaling keep improving capability
Competition among firms and nations prevents slowdown
predictedOutcome: Superintelligence (better than humans in every domain) plausibly by ~2035.
contextAtTime: Reasoning models (o1/o3, DeepSeek-R1) and agents had advanced rapidly in late 2024-early 2025.
outcome: Not resolvable by Oct 2026.
verdictRationale: Horizon not reached.
evolution: Further shortening of the 2023 5-20 year estimate; by Sept 2026 he told senators researchers' timelines were shortening.

claim: AI will replace 'everybody' in mundane intellectual labor; mass job displacement is more likely than not and already starting; physical trades are safer for a long time — 'a good bet would be to be a plumber'.
assumptions: AI capability in cognitive tasks continues to improve
Firms substitute rather than augment labor
Robotics/physical manipulation lags
predictedOutcome: Large-scale displacement of white-collar routine cognitive jobs (paralegals, call centers) before physical trades.
contextAtTime: 2025 saw CEO statements about AI replacing white-collar roles and early evidence of weaker entry-level hiring.
outcome: By 2026 Fortune reports layoffs had not spiked but evidence mounted of AI shrinking entry-level opportunities; no mass unemployment observed as of Oct 2026.
verdictRationale: No dated horizon; early signals are mixed. Note that his 2016 occupation-specific forecast (radiology) failed.
evolution: Generalizes the 2016 radiology claim into a broad labor claim.

claim: Told US senators that Congress has 'Maybe a year, but not much more than a year' to put guardrails on AI before it may be too late.
assumptions: Superintelligence timelines are shortening
Regulation must precede highly capable autonomous systems to be effective
predictedOutcome: If Congress does not act within roughly a year (by ~Sept 2027), effective control may be lost.
contextAtTime: Closed-door briefing convened by Sen. Sanders; House adjourned until after Nov 2026 midterms without AI legislation (single source).
outcome: Horizon not reached as of Oct 11, 2026.
verdictRationale: Deadline after the research cutoff.
evolution: Escalation of his post-2023 regulatory advocacy.

claim: If intelligence is a cake, unsupervised/predictive (later 'self-supervised') learning is the bulk of the cake, supervised learning the icing, and reinforcement learning the cherry.
assumptions: Most useful knowledge can be learned by predicting parts of raw data from other parts
predictedOutcome: Self-supervised learning on unlabelled data becomes the main source of AI capability.
contextAtTime: 2016 successes were mostly supervised (ImageNet) and RL (AlphaGo); self-supervised pretraining at scale was unproven.
outcome: Self-supervised next-token pretraining became the foundation of LLMs (GPT series, 2018-2026), with supervised fine-tuning and RL layered on top — though from 2024 RL for reasoning grew in importance.
verdictRationale: The core claim that self-supervised prediction would provide most of the learned knowledge was borne out — ironically via the autoregressive LLMs LeCun later criticized.
evolution: Retained; he later argued the self-supervision should be in representation space (JEPA) rather than generative token prediction.

claim: Autonomous machine intelligence requires learned world models trained by self-supervision in abstract representation space (H-JEPA), plus planning and objective-driven architecture, rather than generative models.
assumptions: Predicting in representation space avoids the intractability of predicting pixels/tokens
Physical-world understanding is a prerequisite for human-level AI
predictedOutcome: JEPA-style world models eventually outperform generative LLMs on the path to human-level AI.
contextAtTime: Published months before ChatGPT; LLM scaling was gaining momentum (GPT-3, PaLM).
outcome: Meta published I-JEPA (2023) and V-JEPA; LeCun founded AMI Labs (raised $1.03B, Mar 2026) to pursue it. As of Oct 2026 AMI had no product and reported results were not independently validated; LLMs remained dominant.
verdictRationale: Research programme with no deadline; neither vindicated nor falsified by Oct 2026.
evolution: No revision; became the basis of his 2025 departure from Meta.

claim: Auto-regressive LLMs are doomed: because each token carries some probability of error that compounds exponentially with answer length, they cannot be made factual, non-toxic or controllable without an architectural change.
assumptions: Per-token errors are independent and uncorrectable
Training can reduce but not eliminate the error rate
predictedOutcome: Autoregressive LLMs hit a reliability ceiling and are replaced by non-autoregressive, world-model-based systems.
contextAtTime: Weeks after ChatGPT/GPT-4 launches, amid widespread hallucination concerns.
outcome: By 2026 autoregressive LLMs remained dominant and improved markedly on long multi-step tasks via reasoning models that backtrack and self-correct within long chains of thought; hallucinations reduced but not eliminated.
verdictRationale: Reliability problems persisted as he said, but the specific mechanism (independent exponential error compounding) was undercut by models that correct their own errors, and LLMs were not abandoned. The ultimate 'no path to human-level AI' claim remains unresolved.
evolution: Repeated unchanged at NYU in Sept 2025.

claim: Fears that AI poses an existential risk are 'preposterous'; the debate is premature until there is a design for a system that can even rival a cat's learning ability.
assumptions: Current systems are far from animal-level intelligence
Objective-driven systems with guardrails will be controllable
predictedOutcome: AI will not pose an existential threat; safety will be engineered incrementally.
contextAtTime: Weeks after Hinton left Google and the CAIS extinction-risk statement signed by Hinton and Bengio.
outcome: No existential catastrophe as of Oct 2026; labs and Bengio-chaired International AI Safety Report document growing dangerous-capability and deception findings; debate unresolved.
verdictRationale: An opinion about long-run risk; absence of catastrophe to date does not falsify either side.
evolution: No revision found; repeated in WSJ (Oct 2024) as 'complete B.S.'.

claim: Open-source AI is safer and prevents concentration of power; calls by Altman, Hassabis and Amodei for regulation amount to attempted regulatory capture.
assumptions: Openness lets many actors find and fix flaws
Misuse risk from open weights is manageable
predictedOutcome: Open models will not cause catastrophic harm and will keep pace with closed ones.
contextAtTime: Meta had released Llama 2 (July 2023); the UK Bletchley summit and US executive order were imminent.
outcome: Open-weight models proliferated (Llama, DeepSeek, Qwen) and stayed close to the frontier; Meta itself became more cautious about open-sourcing its most capable models from mid-2025 (recalled). Hinton referenced a 2026 'Hugging Face incident' as a 'little Chernobyl' (details unverified).
verdictRationale: Normative claim; evidence cuts both ways and no decisive outcome by Oct 2026.
evolution: No revision found.

claim: 'on the path towards human-level intelligence, an LLM is basically an off-ramp, a distraction, a dead end' — while acknowledging LLMs are useful.
assumptions: Text-only training cannot yield physical-world understanding, persistent memory, reasoning and planning
predictedOutcome: Scaling LLMs will not reach human-level intelligence.
contextAtTime: GPT-4-class models widespread; heavy industry investment premised on scaling LLMs.
outcome: As of Oct 2026 no system is broadly accepted as human-level; LLM-based reasoning/agent systems kept improving and absorbed most investment.
verdictRationale: Not falsifiable until human-level AI is (or is not) reached by some route.
evolution: Hardened over time ('complete BS', Apr 2026).

claim: If Meta's research plan succeeds on schedule, within three to five years there will be systems of a completely different paradigm; within five years nobody in their right mind would use current LLMs as the central component of an AI system.
assumptions: JEPA/world-model research succeeds on the hoped timetable
predictedOutcome: By 2028-2030 a non-LLM architecture displaces LLMs as the core of AI systems.
contextAtTime: Similar 'passing fad' claim made at VivaTech June 2023; DeepSeek-R1 had just been released.
outcome: As of Oct 2026 LLMs remain central; AMI Labs had no product.
verdictRationale: Horizon (2028-2030) not reached; early trend does not favor it but cannot settle it.
evolution: Partly conditional on Meta's plan; after leaving Meta he moved the bet to AMI Labs.

claim: Left Meta after 12 years to found Advanced Machine Intelligence (AMI Labs) to build systems that understand the physical world, have persistent memory, reason and plan; raised $1.03B in March 2026.
assumptions: World models are the next paradigm
Capital can be raised for a non-LLM bet
predictedOutcome: AMI produces world models that outperform LLM approaches on physical-world tasks.
contextAtTime: Meta had reorganized AI under Superintelligence Labs (Alexandr Wang) focused on LLMs/products.
outcome: AMI raised $1.03B at $3.5B pre-money (Mar 2026); by Oct 2026 ~50-60 researchers, no product, results not independently verified.
verdictRationale: Too early to judge the venture.
evolution: Consistent with views held since 2022.

claim: Deep learning must move from 'System 1' pattern recognition to 'System 2' capabilities — reasoning, out-of-distribution generalization, compositional and causal representations.
assumptions: Current deep nets lack systematic generalization
New inductive biases/architectures are needed
predictedOutcome: Next major advances come from adding reasoning and causal structure to deep learning.
contextAtTime: GPT-2 era; scaling laws not yet published (Jan 2020).
outcome: Reasoning became the main frontier theme in 2024-2026 (o1/o3, DeepSeek-R1), but achieved mainly by RL-trained chain-of-thought on LLMs rather than the attention/causal-representation mechanisms he proposed; OOD generalization remains a weakness.
verdictRationale: Correct that reasoning would be the key gap; mechanism largely different from what he proposed.
evolution: Focus shifted from capability research to safety after 2023.

claim: Signed the FLI open letter calling for at least a six-month pause on training systems more powerful than GPT-4.
assumptions: Capabilities were outpacing safety and governance
A coordinated pause was achievable
predictedOutcome: A pause would allow safety protocols and governance to catch up.
contextAtTime: Days after GPT-4's release.
outcome: No pause occurred; labs continued training larger models (GPT-4o, Claude 3, Gemini, GPT-5).
verdictRationale: As an action aimed at achieving a pause, it failed; it did, however, help shift public debate (e.g., CAIS statement, Bletchley summit).
evolution: Moved toward institution-building (International AI Safety Report, LawZero).
audit: Signing a pause letter is advocacy, not a forecast: shown (the advocated pause did not happen) but not scored.

claim: Revised his timeline: having placed human-level AI decades to centuries away, he now estimated roughly 5 to 20 years (with ~90% confidence), and warned that goal-directed superhuman AIs could go 'rogue'.
assumptions: Scaling plus modest algorithmic advances close the gap to human-level
Agency can be added to capable models
predictedOutcome: Human-level AI arrives roughly 2028-2043.
contextAtTime: Post-ChatGPT/GPT-4; Hinton made a similar revision the same month.
outcome: Not resolvable as of Oct 2026.
verdictRationale: Horizon not reached.
evolution: Maintained and intensified in 2024-2026 (International AI Safety Report, LawZero).

claim: Told the US Senate that human-level AI might come within a few years to a couple of decades and urged immediate regulation, licensing, and international coordination.
assumptions: Government action is feasible and effective in time
predictedOutcome: Binding national and international AI safety regulation needed quickly.
contextAtTime: Testified with Dario Amodei and Stuart Russell; EU AI Act under negotiation.
outcome: EU AI Act adopted (2024); no comprehensive US federal AI law as of Oct 2026 (Hinton's Sept 2026 briefing noted no legislation); international effort led to Bengio-chaired safety reports rather than binding treaties.
verdictRationale: Normative governance claim.
evolution: No revision found.

claim: As chair, delivered the first International AI Safety Report synthesising evidence on general-purpose AI capabilities and risks for governments.
assumptions: A shared scientific evidence base improves policy
predictedOutcome: An IPCC-like process informs international AI governance.
contextAtTime: Mandated at the Nov 2023 Bletchley Park summit; presented before the Feb 2025 Paris AI Action Summit, which shifted emphasis away from safety.
outcome: Report published; follow-up updates and a 2026 edition were produced (recalled).
verdictRationale: Institutional action; impact on policy not measurable yet.
evolution: Consistent with 2023 turn.

claim: Superintelligent agents pose catastrophic risks; a safer path is non-agentic 'Scientist AI' that models and explains the world without pursuing goals — launched LawZero (June 2025) to build it.
assumptions: Agency, not intelligence per se, drives the main risks
Non-agentic systems can be competitive and useful (e.g., as guardrails or for science)
predictedOutcome: A non-agentic Scientist AI can serve as a guardrail on agentic systems and accelerate science safely.
contextAtTime: Industry pivot to agents in 2025.
outcome: LawZero founded with ~$30M (recalled); no deployed Scientist AI as of Oct 2026 found.
verdictRationale: Research agenda with no deadline.
evolution: Builds on his 2023 conversion; opposite bet to industry's agent focus.

claim: Frontier models already display deception, cheating and self-preservation behaviours in tests — early warning signs of loss-of-control risk.
assumptions: Behaviours in contrived evaluations indicate dispositions that matter in deployment
predictedOutcome: Such behaviours will become more capable and consequential as agency grows unless addressed.
contextAtTime: Apollo Research scheming evaluations (Dec 2024) and lab system cards reported such behaviours.
outcome: Multiple evaluations documented scheming/deception in test scenarios; no major real-world loss-of-control incident confirmed (a 2026 'Hugging Face incident' referenced by Hinton is unverified here).
verdictRationale: The empirical claim that such behaviours appear in evaluations is supported; the implication about real-world danger is not yet testable.
evolution: No revision found.

claim: If you have a large dataset and you train a very big neural network, success is guaranteed (seq2seq-era statement of the scaling hypothesis).
assumptions: Large networks trained on enough data can learn any function needed
Compute will keep growing
predictedOutcome: Bigger networks on more data will continue to deliver breakthroughs.
contextAtTime: Following AlexNet (2012) and seq2seq translation (2014); mainstream ML still favored smaller models and hand-designed structure.
outcome: Scaling became the dominant strategy from GPT-2/GPT-3 (2019-2020) through GPT-4 and beyond; scaling laws formalised the trend.
verdictRationale: An early, contrarian conviction that was strongly vindicated over 2017-2024.
evolution: Qualified in Dec 2024 ('pretraining as we know it will end') and Nov 2025 ('age of research').

claim: Co-founded OpenAI as chief scientist to pursue AGI.
assumptions: AGI is achievable via scaled deep learning
A mission-driven lab can lead
predictedOutcome: OpenAI becomes a leading AGI lab.
contextAtTime: Left Google Brain; OpenAI launched as a non-profit with ~$1B in pledges.
outcome: OpenAI produced GPT-3, ChatGPT and GPT-4, becoming the leading commercial AI lab.
verdictRationale: The lab he co-founded became central to the field.
evolution: Left in May 2024.
audit: [f31] No source attached for this record; shown, not scored until one is.

claim: Predicting the next token well requires understanding the underlying reality that produced the text — compression is understanding.
assumptions: Good compression of data requires modelling its generative process
predictedOutcome: Better next-token predictors will exhibit increasingly genuine understanding and reasoning.
contextAtTime: Post-GPT-4; directly opposed by LeCun and Marcus who argued LLMs lack understanding.
outcome: LLM capability on reasoning benchmarks rose sharply 2023-2026, but much of the gain came from RL post-training rather than pretraining alone; debate over 'understanding' remains open, and Sutskever himself stressed a generalization gap in 2025.
verdictRationale: Philosophical/technical claim not settled by evidence to date.
evolution: By Nov 2025 emphasised that models generalize dramatically worse than people.

claim: Co-led OpenAI's Superalignment team with the goal of solving the core technical challenges of superintelligence alignment within four years, backed by 20% of OpenAI's secured compute.
assumptions: Superintelligence could arrive within the decade
Automated alignment researchers can be built
predictedOutcome: Core superintelligence alignment problems solved by mid-2027.
contextAtTime: Corporate OpenAI announcement co-authored with Jan Leike.
outcome: The team was dissolved in May 2024 after Sutskever and Leike left OpenAI; the four-year horizon has not elapsed.
verdictRationale: Deadline (2027) not reached, though the programme as constituted ended early.
evolution: Continued the safety-first goal at SSI.

claim: As an OpenAI board member, voted to remove Sam Altman as CEO; days later said he deeply regretted participating in the board's actions.
assumptions: Board oversight could constrain leadership in service of the non-profit mission
predictedOutcome: Leadership change at OpenAI.
contextAtTime: Tension between commercialization and safety at OpenAI.
outcome: Altman was reinstated within five days after employee revolt; Sutskever left the board and departed OpenAI in May 2024.
verdictRationale: The action failed to achieve its aim and was reversed within days.
evolution: Publicly reversed (regret post, Nov 20, 2023).
audit: [f5] A board vote is a governance act, not a claim about AI's evolution; shown, not scored (consistent with as-bengio-2).

claim: Founded Safe Superintelligence Inc. as a 'straight-shot' lab with one goal and one product — safe superintelligence — insulated from short-term commercial pressure.
assumptions: Superintelligence is reachable by a small focused team with a different research approach
Investors will fund years without product revenue
predictedOutcome: SSI develops safe superintelligence without intermediate products.
contextAtTime: Weeks after leaving OpenAI.
outcome: SSI raised ~$1B (Sept 2024) and was reportedly valued ~$32B (Apr 2025); co-founder Daniel Gross left for Meta (July 2025) and Sutskever became CEO. No public product found as of Oct 2026 (unverified for Jul-Oct 2026).
verdictRationale: Venture outcome not yet determinable.
evolution: Consistent with Superalignment-era priorities.

claim: Pre-training as we know it will unquestionably end: compute keeps growing but data does not — 'we have but one internet'; data is the fossil fuel of AI. Future systems will be agentic, reason, and be less predictable.
assumptions: High-quality human-generated data is finite
Returns from pure pretraining scale diminish
predictedOutcome: Labs shift emphasis from scaling pretraining to new axes (reasoning, synthetic data, agents, inference compute).
contextAtTime: Reports in late 2024 of disappointing returns from next-gen pretraining runs; o1 had shown reasoning gains.
outcome: 2025-2026 frontier progress came largely from RL-based reasoning, inference-time compute and agents; GPT-4.5 (Feb 2025) was seen as showing diminishing pretraining returns. Pretraining nonetheless continued at larger scale and was not abandoned.
verdictRationale: Direction (shift to reasoning/agents, data as constraint) proved right; 'end' of pretraining did not occur literally by 2026.
evolution: Extended in Nov 2025 into 'age of research' framing — a revision of his 2014-era 'scale guarantees success' view.

claim: 2020-2025 was the 'age of scaling'; we are back in an 'age of research, just with big computers'. Models generalize dramatically worse than people; systems that learn as well as humans could come in roughly 5 to 20 years.
assumptions: Scaling current recipes yields diminishing returns
A new learning approach can close the generalization gap
predictedOutcome: Next breakthroughs come from new ideas rather than more scale; human-like learners in 5-20 years.
contextAtTime: Industry capex at record levels premised partly on continued scaling; reasoning-model gains continuing.
outcome: Not resolvable as of Oct 2026.
verdictRationale: Long horizon.
evolution: Reversal relative to his earlier scaling maximalism.

claim: Deep learning faces ten fundamental challenges (data hunger, poor transfer, lack of hierarchical structure, weak open-ended inference, opacity, poor integration of prior knowledge, correlation vs causation, etc.) and must be supplemented by other (symbolic) techniques to reach general intelligence.
assumptions: Scale alone cannot overcome these limits
predictedOutcome: Pure deep learning stalls short of general intelligence; hybrids needed.
contextAtTime: Just before GPT-1/BERT (2018) and the pretraining revolution.
outcome: Several challenges (data efficiency, reliability, OOD generalization) remain open; others (transfer, open-ended language inference) improved dramatically through scale. Tool use and code execution in LLM agents add some symbolic components.
verdictRationale: Correctly flagged persistent weaknesses but underestimated how much scale would solve.
evolution: Consistent; restated repeatedly 2019-2026.

claim: Deep learning is hitting a wall: scaling will not deliver reliability or understanding; neurosymbolic approaches are needed.
assumptions: Scaling yields diminishing returns on reasoning and reliability
predictedOutcome: Near-term scaled models would show limited progress on reasoning/reliability.
contextAtTime: Pre-ChatGPT; GPT-3 and early PaLM existed; scaling laws widely accepted.
outcome: ChatGPT (Nov 2022), GPT-4 (Mar 2023) and reasoning models (2024-2025) delivered large measured gains on reasoning and professional benchmarks and massive adoption; hallucinations and reliability issues persisted.
verdictRationale: Measured capabilities rose steeply in the following years, contradicting a 'wall' in 2022; his reliability concerns were partly valid but do not rescue the headline claim.
evolution: Re-asserted in Nov 2024 ('diminishing returns') after pretraining slowdown reports.
audit: Kept incorrect on the headline ('hitting a wall' on capability — rapid gains 2022–26). Auditor noted the parallel LeCun claim (as-lecun-3) is graded partial; the difference is that LeCun's claim concerned reliability/factuality only, while Marcus's headline concerned progress itself.
interpretations: Capability reading: scaling kept delivering through 2026 — the 'wall' did not appear.
Reliability reading: hallucination and robustness problems persisted, which was Marcus's core claim.

claim: Offered Elon Musk a bet that AGI would not arrive by 2029, under specified criteria.
assumptions: Current approaches lack robust understanding
predictedOutcome: No AGI meeting his criteria by end of 2029.
contextAtTime: Musk had said he expected AGI by 2029.
outcome: Not resolvable as of Oct 2026.
verdictRationale: Deadline not reached.
evolution: No revision found.

claim: Testified to the US Senate (alongside Sam Altman) calling for an FDA-like licensing agency, independent audits and international oversight of AI.
assumptions: Self-regulation by AI companies is insufficient
predictedOutcome: Strong external regulation is needed to manage AI risks.
contextAtTime: First major congressional AI hearing after ChatGPT.
outcome: No US federal AI licensing agency as of Oct 2026; EU AI Act adopted.
verdictRationale: Normative claim.
evolution: Later grew more critical of OpenAI/Altman (2024 book 'Taming Silicon Valley').

claim: For 2024: roughly 7-10 GPT-4-level models; no massive advance (no GPT-5-level model); price wars; little moat; no robust solution to hallucinations; modest corporate adoption and profits.
assumptions: Scaling returns slowing
Many labs could replicate GPT-4
predictedOutcome: By end-2024: multiple GPT-4-class peers, no GPT-5, falling prices.
contextAtTime: Gemini announced Dec 2023; Claude 2/Llama 2 below GPT-4; widespread expectation of GPT-5 in 2024.
outcome: 2024 saw many GPT-4-class models (Claude 3/3.5, Gemini 1.5, Llama 3.1 405B, Qwen, DeepSeek-V2/V3), steep API price cuts, no GPT-5 (released Aug 2025), and persistent hallucinations. OpenAI's o1 (Sept 2024) was a notable reasoning advance some would call a substantial leap.
verdictRationale: Most specific components held by end-2024; the o1 reasoning jump is the main caveat.
evolution: Issued follow-on predictions for 2025.

claim: Generative AI could turn out to be an economic 'dud' — its value far below what valuations implied — and the boom resembles a bubble.
assumptions: Hallucinations limit enterprise adoption
Revenue will not justify capex
predictedOutcome: Disappointing revenue relative to investment and a correction in AI valuations.
contextAtTime: Mid-2023 hype after ChatGPT; capex ramp beginning.
outcome: Through mid-2026 AI capex and lab revenues kept growing rapidly; no broad AI market crash had occurred as of the last verified information (Jul-Oct 2026 not verified). Enterprise ROI evidence remained mixed.
verdictRationale: No deadline; a bubble cannot be confirmed or refuted until a cycle completes.
evolution: Repeated through 2024-2025.

claim: GPT-5 was overdue, overhyped and underwhelming; hallucinations and reasoning errors remain unsolved in pure LLMs.
assumptions: LLMs lack world models and robust reasoning
predictedOutcome: LLM scaling will not eliminate hallucinations.
contextAtTime: GPT-5 released Aug 7, 2025 to mixed reviews.
outcome: Hallucinations reduced but not eliminated as of 2026; OpenAI researchers acknowledged structural incentives behind them (Sept 2025).
verdictRationale: Persistence of hallucinations supports him; 'underwhelming' is a judgment, and GPT-5 class models were widely used.
evolution: No revision found.

claim: Neural networks are 'Software 2.0': code 'written in much more abstract, human unfriendly language, such as the weights of a neural network'. Programmers will increasingly specify goals and datasets and let optimization find the program, displacing hand-written code in many domains.
assumptions: Data + compute + gradient descent outperform hand-engineering in more and more domains
Tooling (the 'Software 2.0 stack') matures
predictedOutcome: A growing share of production functionality (vision, speech, translation, control) is implemented by trained networks rather than explicit code.
contextAtTime: 2017: deep nets dominated vision/speech benchmarks. Transformers had just appeared (June 2017). Most production software remained hand-written. Karpathy was replacing Tesla Autopilot heuristics with nets.
outcome: By 2026 learned models dominate perception, speech, translation and language tasks. LLMs became the general substrate, which Karpathy himself relabelled 'Software 3.0' in 2025. Coding agents now write much code.
verdictRationale: The core claim that learned weights would displace hand-written code across many domains held. The mechanism shifted from task-specific training to prompting pretrained LLMs, which he folded into his framework rather than contradicting it.
evolution: Extended to 'Software 3.0' (prompts in English programming LLMs) at YC AI Startup School, June 2025.

claim: "The hottest new programming language is English"
assumptions: LLM code generation keeps improving
Natural-language specification becomes a practical interface for producing working software
predictedOutcome: Natural-language prompting becomes a mainstream way to produce software.
contextAtTime: Two months after ChatGPT. Copilot existed but was autocomplete-level. Most engineers were skeptical of LLM code quality.
outcome: By 2025–26 'vibe coding' and agentic coding tools became mainstream. Karpathy reported in Jan 2026 he was 'mostly programming in English now', with ~80% agent-written code.
verdictRationale: Pithy but directionally falsifiable. Within three years, natural-language-driven coding agents became a dominant developer workflow, though professional use still requires review.
evolution: Expanded into 'vibe coding' (Feb 2025), 'Software 3.0' (Jun 2025) and the agentic-engineering 'phase shift' (Jan 2026).

claim: LLMs should be seen "not as a chatbot, but the kernel process of a new Operating System" that orchestrates tools, memory (context as RAM), browsing, code execution and multimodal I/O.
assumptions: Tool use and long context improve
Ecosystems form around LLM 'kernels' as around OSes
predictedOutcome: LLM products evolve into orchestration platforms that call tools and manage memory, with OS-like ecosystems.
contextAtTime: Sept 2023: ChatGPT plugins, code interpreter and GPT-4V had just shipped. Agent frameworks were immature.
outcome: Tool calling, MCP-style connectors, computer use and agent harnesses became standard in 2024–26. Frontier labs compete as platforms, but no single 'LLM OS' platform dominates.
verdictRationale: The architectural pattern he described (LLM as orchestrator of tools and memory) became mainstream. The OS-like platform-lock-in implication remains contested.
evolution: Reiterated in YC 2025 talk (LLMs as utilities/fabs/operating systems).

claim: Founded Eureka Labs, 'a new kind of school that is AI native': 'The teacher still designs the course materials, but they are supported, leveraged and scaled with an AI Teaching Assistant.'
assumptions: LLMs are reliable enough to tutor at scale
Expert-designed courses plus AI TAs beat either alone
predictedOutcome: An AI-native education product (starting with LLM101n) reaches learners at scale.
contextAtTime: Mid-2024: Khanmigo and other AI tutors were emerging. Karpathy had just left OpenAI.
outcome: Karpathy released educational open-source projects. By May 2026 he joined Anthropic's pretraining team. Eureka Labs' status (paused or continuing) is unclear in coverage.
verdictRationale: No evidence of scaled product outcomes either way, and the founder's move to Anthropic leaves the venture's trajectory uncertain.
evolution: Left to join Anthropic (May 2026). One report says he plans to resume education work later.

claim: There's a new kind of coding, 'vibe coding', where you 'fully give in to the vibes, embrace exponentials, and forget that the code even exists', which works for throwaway projects with LLM coding tools.
assumptions: Coding models are good enough to produce working small apps without line-by-line review
predictedOutcome: Non-review, prompt-driven app creation becomes a viable mode for low-stakes software.
contextAtTime: Cursor Composer, Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet-era tools. Agentic coding just emerging.
outcome: The term went mainstream, and an industry of 'vibe coding' app builders grew in 2025–26. Security and quality concerns accompanied it. Karpathy later distinguished it from disciplined 'agentic engineering'.
verdictRationale: A descriptive claim about an emerging practice that proved widely adopted. He scoped it to throwaway projects, a caveat often lost in later hype.
evolution: By Dec 2025–Jan 2026 he emphasized serious agentic workflows and said he felt 'behind' as a programmer.
audit: [f9] Coining 'vibe coding' described a practice the same day; its spread is self-fulfilling, not foresight.

claim: "When I see things like oh 2025 is the year of agents I get very concerned and I kind of feel like you know this is the decade of agents". Builders should make partial-autonomy products (an 'autonomy slider', humans verifying) rather than fully autonomous agents.
assumptions: Reliability ('march of nines') takes years per step, as in self-driving
LLMs remain fallible and need human verification
predictedOutcome: Fully autonomous, reliable general agents take roughly a decade (≈2025–2035). Near-term value comes from human-in-the-loop tools.
contextAtTime: Industry marketing in 2025 billed it 'the year of agents'. Agent benchmarks were improving, but enterprise deployments were brittle.
outcome: By Oct 2026 coding agents are widely used with human oversight. Fully autonomous general-purpose agents replacing workers are not established. The horizon has not passed.
verdictRationale: The 10-year horizon runs to ~2035. The partial-autonomy advice matches how coding agents were actually adopted, but full autonomy is untested.
evolution: Repeated on Dwarkesh (Oct 2025). Softened for coding specifically in Jan 2026.

claim: AGI and mature agents are still about a decade away. Current agents 'just don't work' as employees: they lack sufficient intelligence, multimodality, computer use and continual learning. RL is 'terrible' (but everything else is worse). AI will likely blend into the existing ~2% GDP growth trend rather than produce a discontinuity.
assumptions: Continual learning and other cognitive gaps need years of research
Diffusion of automation is gradual as with past technologies
predictedOutcome: No AGI or employee-replacing agents before ~2035, and no visible break in GDP growth trend.
contextAtTime: Oct 2025: GPT-5 and Claude 4.x-era models. Lab leaders (Amodei, Altman) talked of powerful AI by 2026–2027. Karpathy explicitly called the estimate intuition.
outcome: Within three months he reported coding agents had crossed a coherence threshold (Jan 2026). By Oct 2026 AGI is not established and no macro GDP discontinuity is documented. The horizon has not passed.
verdictRationale: The deadline is ~2035. His January 2026 update concerns coding agents, not the broader agent/AGI claim, so it is an evolution, not a falsification.
evolution: Jan 2026: 'threshold of coherence... phase shift in software engineering' for coding agents. May 2026: joined Anthropic to use Claude to accelerate pretraining, a sign he now treats AI-accelerated research as near-term.

claim: Camera-only vision with neural networks and fleet data is the scalable path to self-driving. Lidar-based approaches require pre-mapping, and maintaining HD maps is unscalable. In 2025 he cautioned that self-driving is not 'solved' and reliability is a long 'march of nines'.
assumptions: Neural nets can extract depth/velocity from cameras as well as lidar
Fleet data scale compensates for sensor limits
predictedOutcome: A vision-only stack eventually achieves driverless operation at scale more cheaply than lidar+HD-map stacks. Reliability takes many years.
contextAtTime: 2019–2021: Waymo (lidar + HD maps) ran limited driverless service. Tesla dropped radar in 2021. Musk was promising FSD 'this year' annually.
outcome: By late 2025 Tesla ran limited robotaxi service (from June 2025) while lidar-based Waymo scaled paid driverless service. Karpathy said in Oct 2025 'We still haven't declared success' but expects success. Tesla's unsupervised status in 2026 was not verified during research.
verdictRationale: Vision-only has not yet been shown to work at scale unsupervised, nor been shown impossible. His 2025 caution about the 'march of nines' is consistent with observed slow progress. No dated timeline was found to score.
evolution: Shift in emphasis from vision-only optimism (2019–21) to stressing long reliability tails (2025). No explicit reversal on vision-only.

claim: Released 'autoresearch' (an agent autonomously edits training code, runs short experiments and keeps improvements), then joined Anthropic (May 2026) to lead a group using Claude to accelerate large-scale pretraining research.
assumptions: AI agents can productively automate parts of ML research given clear metrics
predictedOutcome: AI agents materially accelerate frontier model training research.
contextAtTime: Early 2026: coding agents had just become reliable enough for long autonomous loops. Labs publicly targeted automated AI researchers.
outcome: autoresearch saw rapid adoption (tens of thousands of GitHub stars) and reported small gains on narrow metrics (e.g., 'time to GPT-2' 2.02h to 1.80h). Impact on frontier pretraining is not yet public.
verdictRationale: Early demonstrations exist only on narrow, single-metric tasks. Frontier-scale acceleration is undocumented as of Oct 2026.
evolution: Represents an update from his Oct 2025 skepticism about agent capability.

claim: Large-scale, diverse labeled data (ImageNet) rather than better hand-designed models is the key to visual recognition. In her 2017 words, 'Data will redefine how we think about models.'
assumptions: Learning algorithms can exploit orders of magnitude more data
Crowdsourced labeling at scale is feasible and accurate enough
predictedOutcome: Models trained on large datasets dramatically outperform prior methods on recognition.
contextAtTime: 2006–2009: computer vision focused on features and models with small datasets (e.g., Caltech-101, PASCAL VOC). The co-author called the data-first idea 'a very bold hypothesis'.
outcome: AlexNet's ILSVRC 2012 win on ImageNet launched the deep-learning era. Data scale became central to all subsequent foundation-model scaling.
verdictRationale: The data-centric bet was contrarian in 2009 and was decisively vindicated by 2012 and by every subsequent scaling wave.
evolution: Later extended the data/grounding argument to 3D spatial data and world models (2024–25).

claim: AI should be 'human-centered': reflect more of the depth of human intelligence, enhance rather than replace humans, and be guided at each step by concern for its human impact. 'there is nothing "artificial" about this technology'.
assumptions: Universities, industry and government coordinate
Designers can choose augmentation over replacement
predictedOutcome: An interdisciplinary, augmentation-focused AI agenda takes hold in research and policy.
contextAtTime: March 2018, while she was Google Cloud chief scientist amid the Project Maven controversy. Ethics-in-AI discourse was growing.
outcome: Stanford HAI (2019) institutionalized the framing and 'human-centered AI' became common policy vocabulary. Industry deployment in 2025–26 increasingly targets labor substitution (agents), so the augmentation goal is contested.
verdictRationale: This is an aspiration, not a forecast. Its institutional uptake is clear, but whether AI is developed as augmentation rather than replacement remains open.
evolution: Consistent through 2025. Reapplied to spatial intelligence ('AI to augment human creativity and robotics').

claim: Co-founded Stanford HAI to advance human-centered AI research, education and policy.
assumptions: Academic institutions can shape AI policy and norms
predictedOutcome: HAI becomes an influential policy and research hub.
contextAtTime: 2019: AI ethics institutes proliferating. Industry dominance of AI research was growing.
outcome: HAI produced the widely cited AI Index and led the NAIRR advocacy coalition. Li served on the federal NAIRR Task Force.
verdictRationale: The implied belief, that an academic center could materially shape US AI policy, is supported by HAI's role in NAIRR and in indicators like the AI Index.
evolution: Li moved her primary focus to World Labs from 2024 while remaining HAI co-director.

claim: The US government should create a National AI Research Resource giving academic and public-sector researchers access to compute and government datasets, because they are falling behind industry.
assumptions: Compute access is the binding constraint for academic AI
A government-funded resource can be built at meaningful scale
predictedOutcome: Without public compute, academia's share of frontier AI research shrinks. With NAIRR, it can remain competitive.
contextAtTime: 2019: training costs rising quickly. GPT-2 era. Academia already struggling to train frontier models.
outcome: The NAIRR Task Force was created (2021) and NSF launched a NAIRR Pilot in January 2024. Frontier model development became overwhelmingly industrial. Full-scale NAIRR funding by Oct 2026 was not verified.
verdictRationale: Her diagnosis that academia would be priced out of frontier AI proved correct. The remedy was adopted only at pilot scale, far below industry compute.
evolution: Repeated in later testimony and in the SB 1047 op-ed (concern for public sector/academia).
audit: [f7] Policy advocacy (NAIRR); outcome partly shaped by the advocacy itself. Treated like other advocacy (licensing calls) — shown, not scored.
unscored: Advocacy; outcome shaped by the advocate.

claim: "If passed into law, SB-1047 will harm our budding AI ecosystem, especially the parts of it that are already at a disadvantage to today's tech giants: the public sector, academia, and 'little tech.'"
assumptions: Developer liability and kill-switch provisions chill open-source release
Developers cannot foresee all downstream uses
predictedOutcome: If enacted, SB 1047 would reduce open-model release and academic/startup innovation.
contextAtTime: Aug 2024: SB 1047 passing the California legislature. Bengio and Hinton supported it. a16z (World Labs' lead investor) led opposition.
outcome: Gov. Newsom vetoed SB 1047 in late Sept 2024. California later enacted the transparency-focused SB 53 (2025), informed by a working group Li co-led.
verdictRationale: The condition (enactment) never occurred, so the counterfactual harm cannot be tested.
evolution: Evolved toward endorsing evidence-based transparency requirements via the 2025 California frontier-AI policy report she co-led (recalled; not re-verified).

claim: Co-founded World Labs ($230M) to build 'large world models' with spatial intelligence that perceive, generate and interact with 3D worlds. The company targeted a first product in 2025.
assumptions: 3D/spatial generation is a distinct capability not delivered by LLM scaling
Markets exist in creative tools, gaming, simulation and robotics
predictedOutcome: World Labs ships a commercial world-model product in 2025, and spatial intelligence becomes a major frontier.
contextAtTime: 2024: Sora previews. LLM scaling dominant. 'World models' a niche topic outside robotics/LeCun's JEPA work.
outcome: Marble launched commercially on 12 Nov 2025. World Labs raised $1B (Feb 2026; Autodesk $200M) and AMD agreed on ~29 Sept 2026 to acquire it for ~$8.2B in stock, with Li to become AMD chief scientist. Product revenue scale is undisclosed.
verdictRationale: The first product shipped in 2025 as planned, and world models became a heavily funded frontier. The strategic bet won strong market validation, though valuation is not proof of realized economic returns.
evolution: Articulated more fully in 'From Words to Worlds' (Nov 2025). Pivoted to hardware-company ownership with the AMD deal (Sept 2026).

claim: Spatial intelligence is AI's next frontier. Language models lack grounding in space, motion and physical consequence (multimodal models rarely beat chance at estimating distance, orientation and size). True world models must be able to generate consistent 3D worlds (her other two required capabilities, recalled as multimodal and interactive, were not confirmed during research).
assumptions: Spatial reasoning won't emerge sufficiently from scaling text/video models
New 3D data and architectures are needed
predictedOutcome: World models become the next major capability wave, enabling robotics, simulation and creative tools beyond LLMs.
contextAtTime: Late 2025: Genie 3, Nvidia Cosmos and others pushing world models. LeCun leaving Meta to pursue world models. LLMs still dominant commercially.
outcome: Investment in world models rose sharply in 2026 (World Labs $1B round, AMD acquisition). LLM-based systems remain the dominant commercial AI. Whether spatial intelligence is 'the' next frontier is undetermined.
verdictRationale: This is an open-ended directional claim. Capital flows support salience but do not establish technical primacy.
evolution: Consistent with her 2024 World Labs thesis and her lifelong vision-first view.

claim: "I frankly don't even know what AGI means." In Nov 2025 she called AGI more of a marketing term than a rigorous scientific one.
assumptions: Scientific rigor requires operational definitions
predictedOutcome: No testable prediction. Rejects AGI-timeline framing.
contextAtTime: 2024–25: lab CEOs (Altman, Amodei, Hassabis) publicly offering AGI timelines.
outcome: No consensus definition of AGI emerged by Oct 2026. Contractual and benchmark definitions proliferated.
verdictRationale: This is a definitional opinion and not falsifiable.
evolution: Hardened from agnosticism (2024) to calling it a marketing term (2025).

claim: The biggest lesson from 70 years of AI research is that general methods that leverage computation are ultimately the most effective, by a large margin, because computation keeps getting exponentially cheaper. Methods building in human knowledge help short-term but plateau and inhibit progress.
assumptions: Moore's-law-like growth in available computation continues
General learning/search methods scale with compute
predictedOutcome: Over time, compute-scaled general methods will beat knowledge-engineered approaches across AI domains.
contextAtTime: March 2019: GPT-2 just released. AlphaZero and deep learning successes in vision/speech. Many researchers still invested in domain-specific inductive biases.
outcome: 2020–2026 scaling (GPT-3/4, scaling laws, RL-on-LLMs, massive data-center buildouts) broadly confirmed that compute-scaled general methods dominate. The essay became a canonical reference for scaling advocates.
verdictRationale: Judged on 2019 information, it was a strong directional bet that the subsequent scaling era bore out. Sutton himself argues LLMs' reliance on human data is only a partial application of the lesson.
evolution: No revision. In 2025 he applied it against LLMs (human-data dependence).

claim: Search and learning are the two general methods that scale arbitrarily with computation.
assumptions: Both training-time learning and inference-time search convert compute into capability
predictedOutcome: Both learning (training) and search (inference-time computation) will be major sources of capability gains.
contextAtTime: 2019: learning-at-scale was ascendant. Inference-time search was mostly associated with game-playing (MCTS).
outcome: From 2024 inference-time compute (o1/o3 reasoning, test-time search on ARC, parallel sampling) became a second scaling axis alongside training.
verdictRationale: The 2024–26 rise of test-time/inference scaling matches his pairing of search with learning. The 'search' is chain-of-thought sampling rather than classical tree search.
evolution: No revision found.

claim: The Alberta Plan: AI research should focus on agents that learn continually, online, from a single stream of experience, building and planning with learned world models.
assumptions: Continual-learning algorithms can be made stable and efficient
Experience-based agents generalize better than static pretrained models
predictedOutcome: Continual, experiential RL agents become the path to general intelligence.
contextAtTime: Aug 2022: pre-ChatGPT, with large language models scaling via static pretraining.
outcome: Continual learning was widely cited by 2025–26 (including by Karpathy) as a key missing capability of LLM agents. Frontier systems still rely on static pretraining plus RL post-training.
verdictRationale: This is a long-run research agenda. Its diagnosis (lack of continual learning) gained mainstream recognition, but the approach is unproven at frontier scale.
evolution: Continued via Keen Technologies and the Era of Experience paper (2025).

claim: Succession to AI (or AI-augmented beings) is inevitable and should be welcomed as the next step in the evolution of intelligence rather than resisted out of fear.
assumptions: Superhuman AI will be built
Value lies in intelligence/complexity rather than specifically human control
predictedOutcome: Humans will eventually be succeeded by AI as the dominant intelligence.
contextAtTime: 2023: Hinton and Bengio raising existential-risk alarms. CAIS extinction-risk statement (May 2023). Pause letter (Mar 2023).
outcome: No succession has occurred. The debate continues, with Sutton among the most prominent researchers rejecting the doom framing.
verdictRationale: This is a long-horizon normative and predictive claim and cannot be evaluated yet.
evolution: No revision found. Venue and date recalled, not verified.

claim: Joined John Carmack's Keen Technologies to pursue AGI through RL-based agents with a small team, outside the LLM mainstream.
assumptions: AGI does not require frontier-scale LLM compute
Experience-driven RL is the right path
predictedOutcome: A small RL-focused lab makes significant progress toward general agents.
contextAtTime: 2023: capital concentrating in LLM labs. Carmack publicly betting on non-LLM paths.
outcome: No breakthrough results from Keen Technologies were documented in during research's research.
verdictRationale: No public results allow evaluation.
evolution: No revision found.

claim: LLMs are a dead end for reaching real intelligence. They imitate what people say rather than learn from experience, have no goal or ground truth, and are not true world models. Systems that learn from experience will supersede them, as the Bitter Lesson implies.
assumptions: Human-data imitation caps capability
Experience-based RL can scale beyond it
predictedOutcome: The dominant paradigm will shift from LLM pretraining to agents learning from experience.
contextAtTime: Sept 2025: reasoning models trained with RL on verifiable rewards were rising (a partial move toward his view). LLM capex was at record levels.
outcome: As of Oct 2026 LLM-based systems remain dominant and continue improving. RL post-training and agentic training environments became increasingly central, blending imitation with experience. No paradigm replacement has occurred.
verdictRationale: No deadline was given. Disagreement from LLM proponents does not falsify it, and LLM progress through 2026 does not confirm it either.
evolution: Consistent with the Alberta Plan (2022) and Era of Experience (2025). Karpathy published a partial rebuttal ('Animals vs Ghosts').

claim: Deep neural networks (policy and value nets) combined with Monte Carlo tree search and RL from self-play can master Go at professional level, a feat previously thought to be a decade away.
assumptions: Learned evaluation can replace hand-crafted heuristics in huge search spaces
predictedOutcome: AlphaGo defeats top human professionals.
contextAtTime: Before 2016 the best Go programs played at strong amateur level. Many experts expected professional-level Go AI to be ~10 years away.
outcome: AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol 4–1 in March 2016.
verdictRationale: The demonstrated method decisively beat the world-class professional, years ahead of expert expectations.
evolution: Generalized to AlphaGo Zero/AlphaZero (2017) and MuZero (2019).
audit: [f2] Announces the authors' own demonstrated result (AlphaGo vs Fan Hui) — track record, not foresight.

claim: An algorithm learning tabula rasa from self-play, without human data or guidance, can exceed systems trained on human expert knowledge (AlphaGo Zero).
assumptions: A perfect simulator/verifier (game rules) provides unlimited grounded reward
predictedOutcome: Self-generated experience can surpass human data where reward is well-defined.
contextAtTime: 2017: deep learning broadly relied on human-labeled data. AlphaGo had used human games.
outcome: Demonstrated in Go, then chess/shogi (AlphaZero). By 2024–26 RL on verifiable rewards (math, code) became a core LLM training technique, though language models still start from human-data pretraining.
verdictRationale: Correct within domains with verifiable rewards, and the idea later transferred to reasoning-model training. Human data remains foundational outside such domains.
evolution: Generalized into the 'Era of Experience' thesis (2025).
audit: [f2] Announces a result already demonstrated in the paper (AlphaGo Zero).

claim: A single general RL algorithm (AlphaZero), given only the rules, can reach superhuman performance across multiple games (chess, shogi, Go).
assumptions: Generality across domains with known rules and simulators
predictedOutcome: AlphaZero beats the strongest specialized engines (Stockfish, Elmo) and AlphaGo Zero.
contextAtTime: Top chess engines relied on decades of hand-tuned evaluation functions.
outcome: Results were published in Science (Dec 2018). Neural-network evaluation was later adopted by mainstream engines (e.g., Stockfish NNUE).
verdictRationale: Demonstrated, peer-reviewed result that reshaped computer chess.
evolution: Extended to unknown-model settings via MuZero.
audit: [f2] Announces a result already demonstrated (AlphaZero).

claim: 'Reward is enough': maximizing reward in a rich environment is sufficient to drive behaviour exhibiting most if not all attributes of intelligence (knowledge, perception, language, social intelligence, generalization).
assumptions: Sufficiently rich environments and capable RL agents exist
Sample efficiency can be overcome
predictedOutcome: General intelligence can emerge from reward maximization alone.
contextAtTime: 2021: GPT-3 showed that self-supervised pretraining on human data, not RL, drove the most general behaviour seen. Critics called the hypothesis unfalsifiable.
outcome: Frontier general capabilities came primarily from self-supervised pretraining, with RL increasingly decisive for reasoning and agentic behaviour (2024–26). No system has shown general intelligence from reward alone.
verdictRationale: This is a broad sufficiency hypothesis with no horizon. The RL post-training trend is consistent with it, but the dominant role of pretraining in 2020–26 is a counterpoint, not a refutation.
evolution: Reaffirmed in 'Era of Experience' (2025).

claim: RL with formal verification (AlphaProof, training on self-generated/auto-formalized problems in Lean), together with AlphaGeometry 2, reaches IMO silver-medal standard: a path to advanced mathematical reasoning.
assumptions: Formal verifiers provide grounded reward for math
Self-play-style RL transfers from games to proofs
predictedOutcome: Formal-RL systems reach top human olympiad performance and beyond.
contextAtTime: July 2024: LLMs performed poorly on olympiad proofs, before OpenAI o1.
outcome: AlphaProof/AlphaGeometry 2 scored 28/42 (silver standard) at IMO 2024, with manual formalization and long compute times. At IMO 2025 a natural-language Gemini Deep Think (and an OpenAI model) reached gold standard within time limits, without formal Lean.
verdictRationale: The 2024 result was real and landmark, and RL proved central. But the next jump came from RL-trained natural-language LLMs rather than the formal-RL route AlphaProof embodied.
evolution: AlphaProof published in Nature (late 2025, recalled). Silver's framing shifted to experience-driven agents generally.
audit: [f2] Announces a result already demonstrated (AlphaProof IMO silver).

claim: Welcome to the Era of Experience (with Sutton): the era of human data is reaching its limits. Agents will increasingly learn from their own long-running streams of experience with grounded actions and rewards, and experiential data will come to eclipse human data.
assumptions: High-quality human data is approaching exhaustion
Environments with grounded rewards can be built at scale
predictedOutcome: The dominant source of capability gains shifts from human-data pretraining to experiential RL.
contextAtTime: Apr 2025: o1/o3 and DeepSeek-R1 had shown RL on verifiable rewards. Concerns about 'peak data' were widespread (Sutskever, Dec 2024).
outcome: Through 2026 labs scaled RL environments and agentic training substantially, but pretraining on human data remains foundational. No clear shift to experience-dominant training is documented.
verdictRationale: This is directional and open-ended. Trends are consistent with it but have not yet borne it out.
evolution: Reportedly acted on by founding a startup in 2026 (low-confidence recall).

claim: Reportedly left Google DeepMind to found Ineffable Intelligence, a startup pursuing experience-driven RL toward superintelligence.
assumptions: Experience-driven RL warrants a dedicated lab outside big tech
predictedOutcome: A new lab advances the Era-of-Experience agenda.
contextAtTime: 2026: wave of researcher-founded labs (e.g., Sutskever's SSI, Murati's Thinking Machines, LeCun's world-model venture).
outcome: Not verified during research.
verdictRationale: Unverified recall and no public results.
evolution: n/a

claim: Released Keras, a minimalist high-level deep-learning API, to make deep learning accessible to every developer.
assumptions: Developer accessibility is the bottleneck to deep-learning adoption
predictedOutcome: Broad developer adoption of deep learning via a simple API.
contextAtTime: 2015: Theano/Caffe/Torch required expertise. TensorFlow was not yet released (Nov 2015).
outcome: Keras became TensorFlow's official high-level API and one of the most-used deep-learning frameworks. Keras 3 (2023) supports JAX/PyTorch/TensorFlow. PyTorch later dominated research.
verdictRationale: Massive adoption validated the accessibility thesis, though PyTorch overtook TF/Keras in research.
evolution: No revision.

claim: An 'intelligence explosion' is impossible. Intelligence is situational and bounded by environment, body and culture, and recursively self-improving systems hit bottlenecks, so progress will be roughly linear rather than explosive.
assumptions: Bottlenecks (data, experiment time, environment) scale with capability
predictedOutcome: No runaway recursive self-improvement.
contextAtTime: 2017: Bostrom-style takeoff arguments prominent in safety circles.
outcome: As of Oct 2026 no intelligence explosion has occurred. AI-assisted AI research has emerged (e.g., Karpathy's autoresearch, Anthropic using Claude to accelerate pretraining), so the question is newly live.
verdictRationale: This is an impossibility claim with no horizon. The absence of an explosion so far is weak evidence, and the claim cannot be confirmed.
evolution: No revision found.

claim: Intelligence is skill-acquisition efficiency, not skill at specific tasks. Benchmarks of task skill can be 'bought' with data/priors and so do not measure general intelligence. ARC measures human-like fluid intelligence and resists approaches without broad generalization.
assumptions: ARC tasks are novel enough that memorization/scale won't solve them
predictedOutcome: ARC remains unsolved by systems lacking efficient generalization, even as conventional benchmarks saturate.
contextAtTime: 2019: GPT-2. Benchmarks such as GLUE were being saturated rapidly.
outcome: ARC-AGI-1 resisted LLM scaling from 2019 to mid-2024 (GPT-4-class models scored low). It fell to o3's test-time reasoning in Dec 2024. ARC became a standard frontier-lab benchmark.
verdictRationale: ARC outlasted many benchmarks through five years of scaling, as he argued. It fell only to systems with explicit test-time adaptation, consistent with his definition.
evolution: Created ARC-AGI-2 (2025) and ARC-AGI-3 to maintain the human-AI gap measurement.

claim: LLMs as trained mostly memorize and retrieve patterns/programs and cannot adapt to genuine novelty. Scaling them will not solve ARC or lead to AGI, and a $1M ARC Prize would show it.
assumptions: Pretraining scale doesn't produce test-time adaptation
ARC private set is unmemorizable
predictedOutcome: Pure LLM scaling will not achieve high ARC-AGI scores.
contextAtTime: June 2024: GPT-4o-class models scored roughly 5–10% on ARC-AGI-1. o1 had not been announced.
outcome: In Dec 2024 o3, an LLM with RL-trained chain-of-thought and heavy test-time compute, scored 75.7% (within budget) and 87.5% (high compute) on ARC-AGI-1. Chollet attributed this to test-time program search, not pretraining scale.
verdictRationale: He was right that pretraining scale alone did not crack ARC. But LLM-based systems did, within six months, via reasoning/test-time compute, which undercuts the stronger 'LLMs won't get there' reading.
evolution: Updated after o3 (Dec 2024), calling it a genuine breakthrough.
interpretations: o3's ARC-AGI-1 score shows LLM-based systems with test-time search can adapt — the strong claim failed.
o3 is not a plain LLM; Chollet argued it validated his view that program search was the missing piece.

claim: OpenAI set back progress toward AGI by roughly 5–10 years, by closing frontier research publication and pulling the field's attention and resources onto LLMs.
assumptions: AGI requires approaches other than LLMs
Open publication drives progress
predictedOutcome: Non-testable counterfactual about research trajectory.
contextAtTime: Mid-2024: frontier labs had stopped publishing details. LLM capex surging.
outcome: Counterfactual. Reasoning models arrived within months, which some read as rapid progress via the LLM path.
verdictRationale: A counterfactual opinion that cannot be falsified.
evolution: Tone softened toward LLM-based reasoning after o3, but no explicit retraction found.

claim: o3's ARC-AGI-1 score is a genuine breakthrough, a step-function increase in test-time adaptation, but passing ARC-AGI does not equal AGI and o3 is not AGI. ARC-AGI-2 will still challenge o3, potentially reducing its score to under 30% even at high compute, while smart humans score far higher.
assumptions: ARC-AGI-2 tasks require compositional generalization beyond o3
predictedOutcome: o3 scores under 30% on ARC-AGI-2.
contextAtTime: Dec 2024: o3 just announced. ARC-AGI-2 in development.
outcome: At ARC-AGI-2's launch (Mar 2025) frontier reasoning models including o3 scored in the low single digits. Later frontier systems with refinement reportedly reached roughly 45–55% by late 2025 (low-confidence recall).
verdictRationale: The specific forecast about o3 on ARC-AGI-2 held by a wide margin. The 'not AGI' judgment is consistent with persistent gaps.
evolution: This was itself an update toward LLM-based reasoning.

claim: Co-founded Ndea (with Mike Knoop) to build AGI via deep-learning-guided program synthesis, arguing it is the missing ingredient for efficient test-time adaptation.
assumptions: Program synthesis + DL yields more efficient generalization than LLM scaling
predictedOutcome: A program-synthesis lab produces systems with superior generalization efficiency.
contextAtTime: Jan 2025: reasoning models ascendant. Chollet had left Google (Nov 2024).
outcome: No major Ndea results were verified during research.
verdictRationale: No public results allow evaluation.
evolution: n/a

claim: ARC-AGI-2 (and the interactive ARC-AGI-3) will continue to expose a large gap between AI and human fluid intelligence: tasks easy for humans remain hard for AI.
assumptions: New task distributions defeat current test-time methods
predictedOutcome: Frontier AI scores on ARC-AGI-2/3 remain well below human performance for a sustained period.
contextAtTime: Mar 2025: o3 near zero on ARC-AGI-2. Lab leaders forecasting rapid AGI.
outcome: Frontier scores on ARC-AGI-2 rose substantially in late 2025 (reported ~45–55% for top systems, low-confidence recall). The ARC Prize 2025 grand prize under compute limits went unclaimed. ARC-AGI-3 and July–Oct 2026 results could not be verified.
verdictRationale: The gap persisted under efficiency constraints but narrowed quickly for unconstrained frontier systems. The verdict is tentative given unverified 2026 data.
evolution: Chollet moved to interactive ARC-AGI-3 to keep the benchmark ahead of systems.

claim: AI will not destroy the world, and in fact may save it.
assumptions: AI systems remain tools without independent goals
Humans keep control over deployment
predictedOutcome: No AI-caused catastrophe. AI benefits (productivity, science, medicine) dominate.
contextAtTime: Published two weeks after the CAIS extinction-risk statement (May 2023) signed by Hinton, Bengio, Altman and Amodei, at the height of the AI-risk debate and calls for licensing.
outcome: No catastrophic AI event by 2026-10-11. Frontier AI is widely deployed. Safety concerns (misuse, cyber, bio uplift) remain actively debated, and the existential claim is not testable yet.
verdictRationale: This is a normative, open-ended claim. The absence of catastrophe so far neither confirms nor refutes the long-run risk argument.
evolution: No revision found. Restated in the October 2023 manifesto and in 2026 ('80-year overnight success').

claim: AI will not cause mass unemployment. Fear of AI taking jobs is the lump-of-labor fallacy, and AI-driven productivity growth will lower prices, raise demand and create new industries and jobs.
assumptions: Historical patterns of technology-driven job creation continue
Demand is elastic enough to absorb productivity gains
AI complements rather than fully substitutes for labor
predictedOutcome: No sustained AI-driven rise in unemployment. Total employment grows as AI diffuses.
contextAtTime: Shortly after Goldman Sachs and others estimated hundreds of millions of jobs exposed to generative AI (2023). Mainstream economists were split.
outcome: Through 2026 there was no mass unemployment: US unemployment was about 4.3% in March 2026, though long-term unemployment was rising. Studies found weaker early-career employment in AI-exposed occupations but no broad disruption of the occupational mix through 2025.
verdictRationale: Evidence through late 2026 is consistent with no mass unemployment, but the claim concerns the long run as AI capability rises, and early signs of displacement among young workers are mixed.
evolution: Reiterated with escalating confidence: an 'AI hiring boom' (November 2024), disruption slowed by licensing and unions (October 2025), job-loss fears 'fake' (April 2026).

claim: The single greatest risk of AI is China winning global AI dominance. The US should push AI into the economy as fast as possible, let big AI companies build freely without regulatory capture, and let open-source AI proliferate without restriction.
assumptions: Open models strengthen the US/Western ecosystem more than they help rivals
Regulation would mainly entrench incumbents
predictedOutcome: Policy that restricts open source or licenses frontier AI would hand advantage to China and incumbents. The US should avoid it.
contextAtTime: Senate hearings (May 2023) with calls for licensing. Meta's LLaMA had just leaked/released. China's frontier models were widely seen as behind.
outcome: The US did not adopt frontier licensing. SB 1047 was vetoed, the Biden executive order was revoked, and the 2025 AI Action Plan endorsed open models. Chinese labs (DeepSeek, Qwen) came to lead open-weight models by 2025, and a16z partners themselves said China was 'winning' open source.
verdictRationale: The policy direction he advocated largely prevailed and China did become a serious AI competitor, validating the salience of the China framing. Unrestricted US open source did not, however, keep the US ahead in open weights.
evolution: After DeepSeek (January 2025) he shifted emphasis to the US actively leading open-source AI so the world does not run on Chinese models.
audit: [f8] Winning a policy argument is not forecasting accuracy; shown, not scored.
unscored: Advocacy; outcome shaped by the advocate.

claim: Any deceleration of AI will cost lives. Deaths AI could have prevented are, in his framing, a form of murder.
assumptions: AI's near-term benefits (e.g. medicine) are large and contingent on speed
Safety-motivated slowdowns produce little offsetting risk reduction
predictedOutcome: Normative stance. Not directly testable.
contextAtTime: Height of the 'effective accelerationism' vs AI-safety debate, one month before the OpenAI board crisis.
outcome: Not testable. The manifesto became a reference text for accelerationists and was widely criticized.
verdictRationale: This is a value claim, not a forecast.
evolution: No revision found.

claim: LLM companies may be in a 'race to the bottom': anyone can scrape the internet and buy GPUs, so selling intelligence could be like selling rice, with thin margins. The alternative is a Google-search-like winner-take-all outcome.
assumptions: Model quality converges across labs and open source
Switching costs between models stay low
predictedOutcome: Either rapidly falling model prices and weak model-layer margins, or a winner-take-all leader.
contextAtTime: Late 2024: GPT-4-class capability had spread to many labs and Llama 3.1. Per-token prices were collapsing. OpenAI had just raised $6.6B.
outcome: Per-token prices kept falling steeply, and DeepSeek intensified price pressure in 2025. Frontier labs nonetheless grew revenue rapidly and raised capital at valuations in the hundreds of billions. Neither pure scenario materialized cleanly.
verdictRationale: Price commoditization at a fixed capability level occurred as described, but frontier-model revenue concentrated in a few labs rather than margins collapsing. He hedged between both outcomes.
evolution: By 2026, secondary summaries have him saying 'the moat is not the model', i.e. value lies around the model.

claim: In May 2024 meetings, Biden-administration officials signaled that AI should be controlled by the government working with a small number of large cooperating companies, and told him not to fund AI startups. This was a key reason he backed Trump.
assumptions: His recollection of the meetings is accurate
predictedOutcome: Continuation of that administration would have led to an oligopolistic, licensed AI sector.
contextAtTime: Post-2024 election. Told on Joe Rogan's and Bari Weiss's podcasts.
outcome: Disputed. Sam Altman called it a 'conspiracy theory', and former officials Bruce Reed and Ben Buchanan said in Politico that the account is not what happened.
verdictRationale: This is a contested account of a private meeting and a counterfactual. It cannot be adjudicated from public evidence.
evolution: No revision found.

claim: Action: with Ben Horowitz, co-signed a joint AI policy statement with Microsoft's Satya Nadella and Brad Smith. It calls for regulation only where benefits exceed costs, support for both open-source and proprietary models, and 'Open Data Commons'.
assumptions: Light-touch, use-focused regulation favors startups ('Little Tech')
predictedOutcome: US policy moves toward cost-benefit and use-based regulation that protects open source.
contextAtTime: After the veto of SB 1047 (September 2024), which a16z had campaigned against. Days before the 2024 election.
outcome: Federal US policy in 2025–26 moved strongly in this direction (Action Plan, executive-order revocation, pushback on state laws). California passed the narrower SB 53.
verdictRationale: Judged as an advocacy bet on policy direction, it largely prevailed. Influence here also shapes the outcome, so it is not pure foresight.
evolution: a16z continued with recommendations for the National AI Action Plan (March 2025) and a 'Little Tech Agenda for AI' (2025).
audit: [f8] Joint policy statement — advocacy, not a forecast.
unscored: Advocacy; outcome shaped by the advocate.

claim: DeepSeek-R1 is AI's Sputnik moment
assumptions: China can reach near-frontier capability at far lower cost despite export controls
predictedOutcome: A US strategic wake-up call and intensified US–China AI competition, especially in open models.
contextAtTime: DeepSeek-R1 (January 20, 2025) matched o1-level reasoning benchmarks with open weights. Nvidia lost about $590B of market cap on January 27.
outcome: Chinese open-weight models (DeepSeek, Qwen and others) became the leading open models by late 2025, with rising download share. US policy and labs (e.g. OpenAI's open-weight release in August 2025) responded. US closed frontier labs still led at the frontier.
verdictRationale: The framing, that DeepSeek marked China's arrival as a serious competitor especially in open models, was borne out by 2025–26 developments.
evolution: Led into his 2025 push for US leadership in open-source AI.

claim: AI job-loss narratives are 'fake'. AI will drive a productivity- and demand-led employment boom, and companies citing AI for layoffs are using it as cover.
assumptions: Productivity gains translate into demand and new job categories quickly
Observed layoffs are not principally AI-driven
predictedOutcome: Employment rises rather than falls as AI adoption grows.
contextAtTime: March 2026 unemployment was 4.3% with rising long-term unemployment. Several firms attributed layoffs to AI. Amodei and Khosla were warning of large displacement.
outcome: As of the cutoff, no clear verdict: aggregate unemployment was not dramatically higher, while early-career weakness in exposed occupations was documented. July–October 2026 labor data could not be retrieved.
verdictRationale: The horizon is unspecified and has not elapsed.
evolution: Consistent with his 2023 claim. The October 2025 version added the institutional-friction argument (licensing, unions).

claim: Eventually, we won't need the average doctor and will have much better and cheaper care for 90–99% of our medical needs.
assumptions: Diagnosis and treatment are largely data/pattern problems
Regulators and patients accept algorithmic care
predictedOutcome: Algorithmic 'Doctor Algorithm' systems take over most routine diagnosis and treatment, sharply reducing need for average physicians.
contextAtTime: Pre-AlexNet (January 2012). IBM Watson had just won Jeopardy! (2011) and was being pitched for medicine. Deep learning was not yet practical.
outcome: By 2026, LLMs and medical AI reached strong benchmark performance on medical exams and some diagnostic tasks, but physicians were not displaced. AI was deployed mainly as assistive tools (scribes, triage), and physician employment kept growing.
verdictRationale: The 'eventually' form is not falsified. Capability trends moved toward his direction, but realized substitution has not occurred. See as-khosla-2 for the dated version.
evolution: Generalized in 2024–26 into economy-wide '80% of 80% of jobs' claims and near-free AI doctors for everyone.

claim: By 2025, automated health care will displace up to 80 percent of physicians' diagnostic and prescription work (machines will replace about 80% of what doctors do).
assumptions: Rapid regulatory acceptance
Health-system workflows and payment adapt quickly
predictedOutcome: By 2025 most diagnostic and prescribing work is done by machines rather than physicians.
contextAtTime: 2012 Health Innovation Summit keynote and related writing. Clinical AI was essentially nonexistent outside rules-based decision support.
outcome: By end of 2025 physicians still performed the vast majority of diagnosis and prescribing. Clinical AI adoption was assistive (ambient documentation, imaging triage), and physician employment grew.
verdictRationale: The dated quantitative target was missed by a wide margin. Capability progress (LLMs passing medical exams) came, but institutional, regulatory and liability adoption barriers were underweighted.
evolution: No explicit retraction found. In 2024–26 the 80% figure reappears as a general labor-capability claim with a ~2030 horizon.

claim: Action: Khosla Ventures wrote a $50M check to OpenAI in 2019, as its first venture investor and the largest initial bet Khosla had made in 40 years, despite governance that made it 'almost impossible to diligence'.
assumptions: OpenAI's capped-profit structure could produce venture-scale returns
Scaling general models would be commercially valuable
predictedOutcome: Implied bet that OpenAI would become an extremely valuable company.
contextAtTime: OpenAI had just created its capped-profit LP (March 2019). GPT-2 had been released, and GPT-3 did not yet exist. Few VCs invested.
outcome: OpenAI became one of the most valuable private companies, with valuations in the hundreds of billions by 2025–26. Khosla Ventures added more exposure via a $405M SPV in 2024.
verdictRationale: Judged as a bet, it was strongly vindicated on paper. Per Atlas rules, this is not proof of a specific personal technical belief.
evolution: Doubled down: backed Altman in November 2023 and raised further OpenAI capital in 2024.
audit: [f19] An investment is never proof of belief; shown on the record, not scored.

claim: Frontier AI is a strategic race (a 'war') with China and should not be open-sourced: 'Would you open source the Manhattan Project?'
assumptions: Open frontier weights materially help Chinese labs
Closed US labs can keep a lead
predictedOutcome: Open-sourcing frontier models would erode the US advantage over China.
contextAtTime: Musk had sued OpenAI (February 2024). Meta was releasing Llama openly. Andreessen and LeCun championed open source.
outcome: Chinese labs reached near-frontier and led open-weight models by 2025 (DeepSeek, Qwen), largely through their own work, with distillation allegations against some. US closed labs kept a frontier lead, and the US also embraced open models in policy.
verdictRationale: He was right that China would be a fierce competitor. The mechanism, that US open-sourcing is what would help China, is not clearly supported, since Chinese open models outpaced US open models.
evolution: No revision found.

claim: 80% of 80% of all jobs, maybe more, can be done by an AI. Dystopian outcomes are societal choices, and UBI-style redistribution may be needed.
assumptions: Capability continues on current trend
