Robotics follows for physical work
predictedOutcome: A large majority of the work in most jobs becomes automatable, pressuring wages and requiring redistribution.
horizon: next ~25 years (essay); later tightened to ~5 years
contextAtTime: After GPT-4o and o1-preview (September 2024). Agentic AI was emerging. Labor-market impact was still minimal.
outcome: By October 2026, AI agents handle meaningful shares of tasks in coding and support, but no economy-wide 80%-of-work automation has occurred.
verdictRationale: This is a capability ('can be done') claim with a horizon that has not elapsed.
evolution: Given a 5-year horizon in 2025 and restated as 'starting in about 2030' in March 2026.

claim: AI will make expertise nearly free: an AI tutor for every child on the planet and physician-level expertise for everyone, at near-zero cost, extending to oncologists, structural engineers and software engineers.
assumptions: Inference cost keeps falling
Distribution reaches low-income populations
Regulators permit AI expert services
predictedOutcome: Free or near-free AI tutors and doctors broadly available globally.
horizon: long run (essay frames the next ~25 years)
contextAtTime: Khan Academy's Khanmigo and early medical LLMs existed. Inference costs were falling fast.
outcome: Free general-purpose assistants (ChatGPT, Gemini, etc.) with tutoring and health-information features were available to hundreds of millions by 2026. Regulated 'AI physician' services were not.
verdictRationale: This is a long-horizon claim. Partial progress on access, but not expert-equivalent regulated care.
evolution: Continuous with his 2012 'Doctor Algorithm' thesis.

claim: Within the next five years, any economically valuable job humans can do, AI will be able to do 80% of it
assumptions: Agent and robotics capability scales quickly
'Able to do' refers to capability, not deployment
predictedOutcome: By about 2030, AI capable of performing 80% of the work in any economically valuable job.
contextAtTime: Reasoning models and coding agents were advancing rapidly. Amodei warned of white-collar job losses (May 2025).
outcome: Deadline not reached as of 2026-10-11.
verdictRationale: The horizon (about 2030) has not elapsed.
evolution: Restated in March 2026 as 'starting in about 2030'.

claim: Calls by incumbents, including leading AI firms, for licensing and new regulators are a classic regulatory-capture play that would pull up the ladder on startups and open source. Silicon Valley must engage Washington to prevent it ('2,851 Miles').
assumptions: Incumbents' safety arguments are at least partly self-interested
Licensing regimes favor large firms
predictedOutcome: If adopted, AI licensing would entrench incumbents and suppress open-source and startup competition.
contextAtTime: Months after Altman's May 2023 Senate testimony proposing a licensing agency, and amid EU AI Act negotiations.
outcome: The US did not adopt AI licensing. Open-weight models proliferated. The policy debate shifted toward Gurley's side after 2024.
verdictRationale: The conditional (licensing entrenches incumbents) was never tested because licensing was not adopted. The opinion was influential, but its counterfactual cannot be checked.
evolution: No revision found (corpus not searched during research).

claim: Open-source AI is an essential competitive and innovation counterweight to a few closed incumbents and should not be restricted.
assumptions: Open models can stay near the frontier
predictedOutcome: Open-weight models remain competitive and pressure prices.
contextAtTime: Llama 2 had just been released (July 2023). Closed GPT-4 led clearly.
outcome: Open-weight models (Llama, DeepSeek, Qwen, gpt-oss) stayed within months of the frontier and drove large price declines in 2024–26.
verdictRationale: Open models did remain competitive and exerted price pressure. Low confidence in exact claim wording.
evolution: No revision found (corpus not searched during research).

claim: Action: among the founding funders of the non-profit OpenAI's initial pledge.
assumptions: Advanced AI is coming and should be shaped by a mission-driven lab
predictedOutcome: OpenAI becomes a leading AI lab.
contextAtTime: DeepMind was dominant after its Google acquisition. Deep learning was succeeding in vision and speech. AGI talk was fringe.
outcome: OpenAI became the defining frontier lab (ChatGPT, 2022) and converted to a for-profit structure in 2025.
verdictRationale: This early support anticipated OpenAI's importance. It is a donation, not proof of a specific forecast.
evolution: Joined OpenAI's board, then left in March 2023 over conflicts.
audit: [f19] A donation is not a forecast; shown, not scored.

claim: Action: co-founded Inflection AI with Mustafa Suleyman and Karén Simonyan to build personal AI (Pi). It raised $1.3B in 2023.
assumptions: An independent lab could train competitive models and win consumers with an emotionally intelligent personal assistant
predictedOutcome: Implied: Inflection becomes a major independent personal-AI company.
contextAtTime: Before ChatGPT. Large-model training costs were rising but frontier competition was still open.
outcome: In March 2024 Microsoft hired the co-founders and most staff and licensed the models (about $650M reported). Inflection pivoted to enterprise, and Pi lost its frontier ambition.
verdictRationale: The implied thesis that an independent consumer personal-AI lab could compete failed within two years, as compute and distribution concentrated. Hoffman may hold other personal beliefs; this verdict covers the action's implied bet.
evolution: See reversal 2024-03. Personal-AI ideas continued at Microsoft (Copilot) under Suleyman.

claim: LLMs like GPT-4 will amplify rather than replace humans, acting as a copilot across professions (education, business, creativity, journalism).
assumptions: Humans remain in the loop
Productivity gains are broadly shared
predictedOutcome: Widespread copilot-style adoption in knowledge work without mass displacement.
contextAtTime: Written with GPT-4 before its public launch. Hoffman was then on OpenAI's and Microsoft's boards, so there is a conflict of interest.
outcome: Copilot-style tools (Microsoft 365 Copilot, GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT Enterprise, Claude Code) were widely adopted by 2026. Labor effects so far are concentrated among early-career workers, without mass displacement.
verdictRationale: Copilot adoption happened, but the 2025–26 shift toward autonomous agents and early-career displacement complicate the 'amplify, not replace' framing.
evolution: Extended in 'Superagency' (2025).

claim: Iterative deployment with broad public participation, not precautionary regulation, is the best path to safe and beneficial AI. AI will give individuals 'superagency' (the 'Bloomer' stance).
assumptions: Feedback from mass use surfaces and corrects harms faster than ex-ante rules
predictedOutcome: Broad deployment yields net benefits and manageable harms.
contextAtTime: Published the week of DeepSeek-R1 and days after the Biden AI executive order was revoked.
outcome: US policy embraced deployment-first approaches in 2025–26. The net-benefit claim is not yet testable.
verdictRationale: This is a normative and long-run claim.
evolution: Continuous with 'Impromptu' (2023).

claim: Action: co-founded Manas AI with Siddhartha Mukherjee to use AI to accelerate cancer drug discovery.
assumptions: AI can materially compress drug discovery timelines
predictedOutcome: Implied: faster drug candidate discovery.
contextAtTime: AlphaFold's Nobel Prize (October 2024). Many AI drug-discovery startups, with few approved AI-discovered drugs.
outcome: No public evidence of clinical outcomes by the cutoff was retrieved.
verdictRationale: Drug development horizons extend well beyond 2026.
evolution: No revision found.

claim: Unlike most markets, generative AI was getting less clear over time. A central open question was whether foundation models become an oligopoly aligned with the big cloud providers, and what role open source plays.
assumptions: Training costs keep rising, favoring capital-rich players tied to clouds
predictedOutcome: The model layer consolidates into a few lab–cloud pairs (e.g. OpenAI–Microsoft, Anthropic–Amazon/Google, Google), with open source as wildcard.
contextAtTime: Gemini 1.0 and Mixtral had been released, and Claude 3 was imminent. Many well-funded model startups existed (Inflection, Adept, Character).
outcome: By 2026 the frontier was dominated by a handful of labs tied to hyperscalers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, plus xAI and Meta), with Chinese open-weight labs as the main other force. Several 2023-era model startups were acqui-hired (Inflection, Adept, Character).
verdictRationale: The oligopoly-plus-open-source structure he flagged largely materialized. He posed it partly as a question, which lowers specificity.
evolution: Later posts reportedly describe markets 'clarifying' (not verified during research).
audit: [f18] Posed explicitly as an open question — not scorable as a correct opinion.

claim: Action: reportedly co-led Harvey's Series B, a bet that vertical application-layer AI companies can build durable value on top of foundation models.
assumptions: Domain workflow, data and distribution create moats above the model layer
predictedOutcome: Implied: Harvey becomes a leading legal-AI company.
contextAtTime: Debate over whether 'GPT wrappers' could survive model improvements.
outcome: Harvey became one of the most highly valued legal-AI companies by 2025 (recalled, not re-verified).
verdictRationale: On paper the bet was vindicated, but evidence is recalled only and an investment is not a personal forecast.
evolution: No revision found.
audit: [f19] An investment is not a forecast; shown, not scored.

claim: The singularity, with machine intelligence surpassing humanity and improving itself, will become reality within ~30 years (by 2047), when a single chip will have an 'IQ' of ~10,000.
assumptions: Transistor counts and chip capability keep scaling exponentially
Raw hardware parity with neurons translates into general intelligence
predictedOutcome: By 2047, AI systems surpass the most intelligent humans and self-improve.
contextAtTime: Feb 2017: before the transformer paper, shortly after AlphaGo. The 2045–2050 singularity date was a Kurzweil-derived meme, not mainstream ML consensus.
outcome: Not yet evaluable. By 2026 frontier LLMs exceeded humans on many benchmarks but did not self-improve autonomously. Son himself later shortened his timelines sharply.
verdictRationale: The horizon is 2047. The 'IQ 10,000 chip' is not operationalised.
evolution: Shortened to AGI within 10 years (Oct 2023), ASI within 10 years (June 2024), AGI in 2–3 years (Oct 2024) and 'much earlier' (Feb 2025).

claim: SoftBank's Vision Fund disposed of its entire ~$3.6B Nvidia stake in January 2019 after Nvidia's crypto-driven share-price collapse.
assumptions: Nvidia's near-term upside was limited after the crypto bust (implied by the exit; motive also included locking in profit and Vision Fund structure)
predictedOutcome: Implied: holding Nvidia offered less value than redeploying the capital.
contextAtTime: Nvidia had fallen from ~$292 to ~$153 as crypto-mining GPU demand collapsed. Data-center AI revenue was still small relative to gaming.
outcome: Nvidia later became the defining AI-infrastructure winner. SoftBank re-accumulated a stake and sold it again in Oct 2025 for ~$5.83B.
verdictRationale: Even judged on 2019 information, Son was publicly calling AI the defining revolution, yet the fund sold the main AI-compute supplier at a cyclical low. In hindsight the exit forfeited very large gains. This is a fund action, not a statement of personal belief.
evolution: SoftBank later rebuilt an Nvidia position and fully exited again in Oct 2025, this time to fund OpenAI.
audit: [f19] A divestment is a financial position, not a stated forecast; shown, not scored.

claim: AGI, which he defined as ten times the intelligence of all humanity combined, will arrive within 10 years. ASI 10,000 times smarter than humans will arrive in about 20 years.
assumptions: LLM capability gains continue to scale
'Intelligence multiple of humanity' is a meaningful measure
predictedOutcome: AGI (by his definition) by ~2033; ASI by ~2043.
contextAtTime: Months after GPT-4. Son said he might be the only person who believed AGI was within a decade, though some lab leaders were already giving similar ranges.
outcome: Not yet evaluable as of Oct 2026.
verdictRationale: The horizon has not passed, and his definition is not operationalised.
evolution: Shortened within a year to 2–3 years for AGI.

claim: Artificial super intelligence, 10,000 times smarter than humans, will arrive within 10 years, and AGI (1–10x human) within 3–5 years.
assumptions: Continued exponential capability scaling
Multiple models cooperating 'like neurons' yields superintelligence
contextAtTime: Mid-2024: GPT-4o/Claude 3 era. Lab leaders were floating AGI by 2026–2030; ASI-in-10-years was an outlier claim among investors.
outcome: Not yet evaluable. At the June 2026 AGM he said he aims to achieve ASI 'in his 70s'.
verdictRationale: The horizon has not passed. The '10,000x' figure is rhetorical.
evolution: Repeated through 2025–2026 as SoftBank's corporate mission (top ASI platform within 10 years).

claim: AGI will arrive within the next two to three years. In Feb 2025 he revised this to 'much earlier' than that.
assumptions: Reasoning/agent models keep improving at the 2024 pace
predictedOutcome: AGI by roughly late 2026 to 2027, or earlier per the Feb 2025 revision.
contextAtTime: OpenAI o1 (Sept 2024) had just launched. Altman and Amodei were also signalling AGI-like systems in 2026–2027.
outcome: As of Oct 2026 no consensus AGI had been declared. Frontier labs reported rapid revenue growth (e.g. OpenAI ~$50–70B annualized), but definitions remain contested.
verdictRationale: The upper end of the window (late 2027) has not passed. The 'much earlier' variant is looking strained, but AGI is undefined, so it cannot be falsified yet.
evolution: Compressed further in Feb 2025 ('much earlier'). By June 2026 the rhetoric had moved to ASI 'in his 70s'.

claim: Stargate will invest $500B in US AI infrastructure over four years, deploying $100B 'immediately', with SoftBank holding financial responsibility and Son as chairman.
assumptions: SoftBank and partners can raise equity and debt at unprecedented scale
Power, sites and chips can be secured fast enough
OpenAI demand justifies the capacity
predictedOutcome: $100B deployed promptly and $500B by ~2029, with SoftBank-led multi-GW capacity.
contextAtTime: SoftBank had about $24B of cash. Musk publicly doubted the backers had the money.
outcome: By July 2025 Stargate had reportedly closed no data-center deal, and SoftBank and OpenAI disagreed over sites. OpenAI then announced ~7 GW planned and >$400B of commitments (Sept 2025), mostly with Oracle. By Sept 2026 the Oracle-built Abilene campus (no SoftBank involvement) was ~75% delivered. The SoftBank-linked Milam County site was still under construction (1.2 GW projected by 2028), and Lordstown had ~0 GW. SoftBank and OpenAI each put $500M into SB Energy in Jan 2026.
verdictRationale: The 'Stargate' brand did attract hundreds of billions of commitments, but SoftBank's own capacity delivery lagged badly behind the '$100B immediately' rhetoric. Most operating capacity came from Oracle and OpenAI deals. The 4-year horizon is unfinished, so this is a mid-course partial.
evolution: No public retreat by Son. SoftBank shifted to direct OpenAI equity ($64.6B total) and SB Energy as its main channels.
audit: [f14] Aspiration with a 2029 horizon — unresolved.

claim: Concentrate SoftBank's capital on OpenAI: commit up to $40B (Mar 2025), sell the entire Nvidia stake (~$5.83B, Oct 2025) and part of T-Mobile to fund it, then invest a further $30B (completed Oct 2026).
assumptions: Value accrues to the leading frontier-model company more than to chip suppliers
OpenAI's revenue growth can justify a valuation of hundreds of billions of dollars
predictedOutcome: Implied: an OpenAI stake will outperform a diversified AI-infrastructure position such as Nvidia.
contextAtTime: 2025: OpenAI's revenue was growing fast, but it was burning cash and DeepSeek had raised commoditization fears. Analysts said the Nvidia sale was a funding need, not a bearish signal.
outcome: By Oct 1, 2026 SoftBank had invested $64.6B for about 13% of OpenAI, valued at $852B in the latest round. OpenAI's annualized revenue was ~$50B at end-Sept 2026, with ~$70B expected by year-end.
verdictRationale: The mark-to-market valuation rose, but the bet is unrealized and depends on OpenAI's long-run economics. The investment is a corporate action and not proof of a specific personal forecast.
evolution: Escalated steadily: $40B commitment, then the Nvidia sale, $22.5B (Dec 2025) and $30B more (2026). One less clearly sourced report says Son described the Nvidia sale as reluctant.
audit: [f19] Capital concentration in OpenAI is a financial position.

claim: SoftBank aims to become the biggest platform provider for artificial super intelligence within the next 10 years.
assumptions: ASI arrives within the decade
SoftBank's portfolio (Arm, OpenAI stake, Stargate) forms a coherent platform
predictedOutcome: By ~2035 SoftBank is the leading ASI platform provider.
contextAtTime: Post-Stargate, with the OpenAI commitment in place. SoftBank's holdings were largely financial stakes rather than operated platforms.
outcome: Not yet evaluable.
verdictRationale: Aspiration with a 2035 horizon.
evolution: Reaffirmed in June 2026, when he pledged to lead SoftBank for 10–15 more years to pursue ASI.

claim: AI is still at an early stage, and calling it a bubble is 'an insult to AI' and 'blasphemy against AI'.
assumptions: AI revenue will grow into current capex and valuations
The internet analogy holds (early skepticism, later vindication)
predictedOutcome: No AI bust: valuations and investment are justified by future returns.
contextAtTime: June 2026: hyperscaler capex heading toward ~$700B+ for the year, rising investor scrutiny, and SoftBank's own share price heavily tied to OpenAI.
outcome: Through Oct 2026 capex guidance kept rising (Alphabet, Amazon raised in July 2026) amid investor skepticism and Alphabet's first negative free-cash-flow quarter. No bust had occurred by the cutoff.
verdictRationale: This is an opinion with no horizon. Son is also heavily conflicted, since SoftBank's value depends on OpenAI.
evolution: Consistent with his 2024–2025 rhetoric.

claim: AI training costs have been falling ~70% a year (GPT-3-level training fell from $4.6M in 2020 to $450K in 2022) and should keep falling at that rate through 2030.
assumptions: Wright's-law hardware cost declines continue
Algorithmic efficiency gains compound
Cost measured per fixed capability level, not total frontier spend
predictedOutcome: The cost to reach a fixed capability level falls ~70% a year through 2030.
contextAtTime: Shortly after ChatGPT. Epoch-style algorithmic-efficiency estimates existed, but most commentary focused on rising frontier training budgets.
outcome: Per-capability costs fell sharply. ARK itself reported >99% inference-cost declines in a year by 2026, and efficient models such as DeepSeek-V3/R1 reached near-frontier quality cheaply. Total frontier training and capex spending rose dramatically (hyperscaler capex ~$700B+ in 2026).
verdictRationale: The horizon is 2030. The directional trend for per-capability cost appears on track, but no independent 2026 measurement of the exact annual rate was verified during research.
evolution: Raised to ~75% a year in Big Ideas 2024 (53% hardware, 47% algorithmic).

claim: If vendors capture 10% of the value their products create, AI software could generate up to $14T in revenue and $90T in enterprise value in 2030, with software spend growing at a 42% CAGR from just under $1T.
assumptions: AI drives large knowledge-worker productivity gains
Vendors capture ~10% of value created
predictedOutcome: AI software revenue up to $14T in 2030.
contextAtTime: 2022–early 2023: AI software revenue was tiny and ChatGPT was newly launched. The figure was far above any mainstream forecast.
outcome: By Oct 2026 the two largest model vendors had annualized revenue of roughly $50–70B (OpenAI) and ~$65B (Anthropic, July 2026). That is fast growth, but orders of magnitude below a $14T end-state, and global software spend has not compounded at 42% a year.
verdictRationale: The 2030 horizon has not been reached, and the claim is conditional ('up to'). The 2026 trajectory makes the upper bound look very unlikely, but that does not falsify it yet.
evolution: Big Ideas 2026 shifted emphasis to infrastructure investment (~$1.4T by 2030) and GDP acceleration.

claim: AI should increase the productivity of knowledge workers more than 4-fold by 2030.
assumptions: Rapid enterprise adoption
AI tools substitute for large shares of knowledge tasks
predictedOutcome: Knowledge-worker output per worker more than 4x 2022 levels by 2030.
contextAtTime: Early 2023: anecdotal Copilot/ChatGPT productivity studies only.
outcome: No macro productivity surge of that magnitude was visible by 2026. Labor-market studies found little broad disruption through late 2025.
verdictRationale: The horizon is 2030. The 2026 evidence points well short of the trajectory, but the claim is not falsified.
evolution: Later ARK framing moved to GDP growth (>7% by 2030) rather than per-worker multiples.

claim: ARK's flagship ARKK sold its entire Nvidia position (sales from Nov 2022, full exit Jan 2023), citing a very high valuation and profit-taking after a ~150-fold gain.
assumptions: Nvidia's valuation already reflected AI upside
Better risk-adjusted AI exposure existed elsewhere (software, Tesla)
predictedOutcome: Implied: Nvidia would underperform ARK's alternative AI holdings.
contextAtTime: Late 2022: Nvidia was down sharply from its 2021 peak and ChatGPT had just launched. The data-center AI demand surge was not yet visible in Nvidia's guidance (it came in May 2023).
outcome: Nvidia rallied enormously from 2023 onward. Estimates of ARKK's forgone gains range from >$200M to ~$1.2B. ARKK bought Nvidia again in April 2025.
verdictRationale: The implied view that AI upside was priced in was contradicted within months. Her re-entry in 2025 is a tacit acknowledgment.
evolution: Re-entered in April 2025.
audit: [f19] A divestment is a financial position; her stated valuation view (as-wood-5) is scored instead.

claim: Nvidia, at ~25x expected revenue, is 'priced ahead of the curve'.
assumptions: Nvidia's AI revenue would not grow fast enough to justify its multiple
GPUs are cyclical
predictedOutcome: Nvidia's valuation would stall or correct relative to fundamentals.
contextAtTime: Days after Nvidia's blowout May 2023 guidance, with the stock up ~172% year-to-date.
outcome: Nvidia's revenue and stock kept rising sharply through 2024–2025, and ARK re-bought in 2025.
verdictRationale: Data-center revenue growth outran the multiple, so the valuation was not 'ahead of the curve' over the following two years.
evolution: Early 2024 she still called Nvidia cyclical and expectations possibly ahead of themselves (secondary, WSJ podcast; not in evidence list). She reversed in April 2025.

claim: Software providers will be the next AI beneficiaries after Nvidia: for every $1 of hardware Nvidia sells, software/SaaS providers will generate $8 of revenue.
assumptions: Platform-shift analogies (PC/internet) hold, so apps capture most value
Incumbent SaaS vendors (UiPath, Twilio, Teladoc) can capture AI value
predictedOutcome: AI software revenue becomes a large multiple (~8x) of AI hardware revenue, and the named software stocks benefit.
contextAtTime: Mid-2023: a common analogy to past platform cycles. Cahn's $200B essay (Sept 2023) would soon highlight the opposite imbalance.
outcome: Through 2026, spending stayed concentrated in infrastructure (hyperscaler capex ~$700B+ in 2026). Leading model vendors' revenue (~$50–70B OpenAI, ~$65B Anthropic run-rates) remained far below a multiple of hardware spend. Revenue accrued mainly to model labs rather than the incumbent SaaS names she cited; their stock performance was not verified during research.
verdictRationale: No horizon was given. So far the realized ratio is nowhere near 8:1 and value accrued to labs and infrastructure, which points against the claim, but it is a long-run structural claim.
evolution: No revision found.

claim: The AI cycle is very different from the tech/telecom bubble; worries about a bubble reassure her. In Jan 2026: 'the bubble today is not in AI, but in gold.'
assumptions: AI cost declines unlock demand faster than capex grows
Widespread skepticism means no euphoric top
predictedOutcome: No AI-driven market bust.
contextAtTime: Late 2025: widespread AI-bubble debate, circular-financing concerns and SoftBank's Nvidia exit.
outcome: As of Oct 2026 no AI bust had occurred. Capex kept rising, with investor scrutiny increasing (July 2026).
verdictRationale: This is an opinion with no horizon, and it is not falsified so far.
evolution: Consistent with her long-standing optimism.

claim: ARK Big Ideas 2026: global data-center system investment (~$500B in 2025) could reach ~$1.4T by 2030, and AI-driven acceleration could push global real GDP growth above 7% by 2030.
assumptions: Inference cost declines keep driving demand
Capex translates into productivity at macro scale
predictedOutcome: ~$1.4T annual data-center investment and >7% global real GDP growth by 2030.
contextAtTime: Early 2026: the IMF projected ~3.1% global growth. Hyperscaler capex guidance was rising rapidly.
outcome: Investment is tracking toward the capex part: four US hyperscalers alone guided ~$700–750B for 2026. No GDP acceleration was evident by Oct 2026.
verdictRationale: The horizon is 2030. Capex is on or ahead of path, while the GDP leg is highly contrarian and untested.
evolution: Escalation of earlier ARK GDP forecasts. A secondary report of 'double-digit' GDP growth was not corroborated.

claim: AGI by 2027 is strikingly plausible: counting orders of magnitude in compute, algorithmic efficiency and 'unhobbling' implies another GPT-2-to-GPT-4-sized jump by 2027, yielding models that can do the work of AI researchers and engineers.
assumptions: Compute scaling of ~0.5 OOM/yr continues
Algorithmic efficiency gains of ~0.5 OOM/yr continue
Unhobbling (agents, long context, tool use) converts raw capability into autonomous work
No data wall
predictedOutcome: By ~2027, AI systems can substitute for remote AI researchers and engineers.
contextAtTime: June 2024: GPT-4o/Claude 3 era, before o1 reasoning models. Many researchers (e.g. LeCun, Marcus) disputed straight-line extrapolation.
outcome: Not evaluable yet. By 2026 reasoning and agentic coding models advanced substantially and labs reported very large revenue growth, but no consensus AGI or full automation of AI research had been demonstrated by Oct 2026.
verdictRationale: The 2027 horizon has not passed. He hedged with 'plausible', not certain.
evolution: No public revision found.

claim: The largest AI training clusters will reach ~1 GW (costing tens of billions of dollars) around 2026.
assumptions: Investment keeps scaling ~0.5 OOM/yr
Power can be procured at GW scale
predictedOutcome: At least one ~1 GW AI cluster or campus in operation or near-complete by ~2026.
contextAtTime: Mid-2024: the largest clusters were ~100k H100s (~100–150 MW). GW-scale talk was viewed as speculative.
outcome: The Abilene Stargate campus (1.2 GW planned) was ~75% delivered by Sept 2026 per a tracker, and Epoch put it at ~0.3 GW operating in spring 2026 with completion in Q4 2026. Multiple GW-scale sites were under construction.
verdictRationale: A ~1 GW-class AI campus was largely delivered in 2026, close to his schedule. The caveat is that 'single training cluster' and 'campus' are not identical, and figures vary by source.
evolution: No revision found.
interpretations: ~1 GW-class campuses (e.g. Stargate Abilene) were operating or under construction in 2026 — on track.
Single training clusters at a true 1 GW draw are hard to verify from public data.

claim: Training clusters will scale to ~10 GW (hundreds of billions of dollars) around 2028 and ~100 GW (a 'trillion-dollar cluster') around 2030.
assumptions: AI revenue justifies continuing ~0.5 OOM/yr investment growth
US can add ~20%+ to electricity generation
predictedOutcome: A ~10 GW cluster by ~2028 and a ~100 GW / >$1T cluster by ~2030.
contextAtTime: Widely seen as extreme in 2024.
outcome: As of 2026, the Stargate program was projected to exceed ~9 GW across seven US sites by 2029 (Epoch). That is aggregate across sites, not a single cluster.
verdictRationale: Horizons are 2028 and 2030.
evolution: No revision found.

claim: Total annual AI investment will rise from roughly $150B (2024) to about $500B by 2026, ~$2T by 2028 and ~$8T by 2030.
assumptions: Revenue growth (e.g. a big tech firm reaching ~$100B AI revenue around mid-decade) sustains capex
Capital markets fund the buildout
predictedOutcome: ~$500B of annual AI investment in 2026.
contextAtTime: Big-4 capex was ~$150–200B in 2023–24. Cahn's essay the same month argued revenue would not justify even that.
outcome: 2026 capex guidance for Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta alone was roughly $700–750B, though not all of it is AI-specific.
verdictRationale: The 2026 checkpoint was met or exceeded. The later checkpoints (2028/2030) remain unresolved. The table values are recalled, hence medium confidence.
evolution: No revision found.
audit: Aschenbrenner's ~$500B/yr by 2026 counted total AI investment; the match uses big-four capex guidance (~$700B), a narrower but larger measure — directionally correct.

claim: Power, not chips, will become the binding constraint on AI scaling. The US must rapidly expand electricity generation and should build clusters in the US rather than in Middle Eastern autocracies.
assumptions: Chip supply scales faster than grid capacity
Regulatory permitting is slow
predictedOutcome: Power availability and interconnection become the main bottleneck for AI data centers by the mid-2020s.
contextAtTime: Mid-2024: power was emerging as a concern (e.g. nuclear PPAs), but GPU supply was still the headline constraint.
outcome: By 2025–2026, power procurement and construction drove data-center delays and site choices (Stargate's SB Energy deals; expansions dropped or reallocated). Hyperscalers also cited memory costs and capacity constraints.
verdictRationale: Power did become a central constraint. However, chip and memory supply and financing also bound, and the policy recommendation not to build in the Middle East was not followed (not verified during research).
evolution: No revision found.

claim: Once AGI automates AI research, hundreds of millions of automated researchers could compress a decade of algorithmic progress into a year or less, producing superintelligence by the end of the decade.
assumptions: AGI-level research agents arrive ~2027
Compute for experiments is not the binding constraint
Research progress is largely parallelizable
predictedOutcome: Superintelligence by ~2030.
contextAtTime: An intelligence-explosion argument rooted in long-running rationalist and Good-style reasoning, applied with specific compute numbers.
outcome: Not evaluable as of Oct 2026.
verdictRationale: Conditional and long-horizon.
evolution: No revision found.

claim: Frontier labs' security is grossly inadequate, and the CCP is likely to steal key algorithmic secrets and weights. Theft plus outbuilding on power is China's main path to staying in the AGI race.
assumptions: US labs hold decisive algorithmic secrets
Export controls constrain Chinese compute
predictedOutcome: China's frontier competitiveness would depend mainly on espionage and stolen weights rather than indigenous innovation.
contextAtTime: Mid-2024: Chinese models were viewed as clearly behind, and export controls were tightening.
outcome: DeepSeek-V3/R1 (Dec 2024–Jan 2025) reached near-frontier reasoning performance with documented indigenous efficiency innovations, published openly. US–China benchmark gaps narrowed to near parity in 2024 data. Distillation allegations arose but were not verified during research.
verdictRationale: He was right that China would stay close. His mechanism, which emphasised theft over indigenous efficiency and open publication, did not match what was publicly observed.
evolution: No revision found.

claim: By around 2027/28 the US government will launch a national-security AGI effort ('The Project'), because no startup can handle superintelligence.
assumptions: AGI progress becomes evident to national-security establishments
US–China rivalry intensifies
predictedOutcome: A government-led or government-controlled AGI project by ~2028.
contextAtTime: Mid-2024: no such program existed, and policy discussion centred on export controls and safety institutes.
outcome: Not evaluable as of Oct 2026. Stargate (Jan 2025) was a privately financed effort announced at the White House, not a government-run project.
verdictRationale: The horizon has not been reached.
evolution: No revision found.

claim: Founded Situational Awareness LP, an AGI-thesis investment fund, after leaving OpenAI.
assumptions: Public markets underprice the AGI infrastructure buildout
predictedOutcome: Implied: AI-infrastructure and power-related equities would outperform.
contextAtTime: Launched alongside the essay and podcast in mid-2024.
outcome: Fund size and performance were not verified during research.
verdictRationale: No verified performance data. An investment is not proof of belief beyond the essay's stated thesis.
evolution: No revision found.
audit: [f19] Founding a fund is a financial position.

claim: Annual GPU capex implies ~$200B of AI revenue is needed to pay it back, leaving a '$125B hole that needs to be filled for each year of CapEx at today's levels.'
assumptions: GPUs are ~half of data-center cost
End users need ~50% gross margin
Capex must be paid back by end-customer AI revenue within a short cycle
predictedOutcome: Unless AI revenue rises by over $100B a year, the capex cycle would face a revenue shortfall.
contextAtTime: Sept 2023: OpenAI was at ~$1–2B run-rate and Nvidia data-center revenue was surging. Few investors had quantified the gap.
outcome: By 2026 the two leading labs alone reached ~$50–70B (OpenAI) and ~$65B (Anthropic) annualized revenue, so the 2023-sized hole has been largely filled in run-rate terms. Capex grew several-fold (~$700B+ in 2026), so the required revenue under his method also rose.
verdictRationale: The arithmetic was a fair snapshot, and revenue did surge to roughly fill the 2023-sized gap. The framing underestimated how fast revenue (and capex) would grow, and the gap moved rather than closing.
evolution: Updated to $600B (June 2024). A secondary profile mentions a later ~$840B update.

claim: AI's $600B question: doubling Nvidia's data-center run-rate for total cost, then doubling again for end-user margin, implies ~$600B of annual AI revenue is needed. Even with generous assumptions there is a ~$500B gap.
assumptions: Same cost-stack multipliers as 2023
Revenue must come from end-customer AI products within the hardware's useful life
predictedOutcome: Absent ~$600B/yr of AI revenue, investors in the buildout face losses (he called this 'investment incineration').
contextAtTime: June 2024: Nvidia's data-center revenue was exploding while AI-native revenue was ~$10B-scale. The same month Aschenbrenner argued investment would scale to $1T clusters.
outcome: By Oct 2026 AI revenue had grown enormously (OpenAI ~$50–70B and Anthropic ~$65B annualized), but remained far below $600B. Capex kept increasing to ~$700B+ in 2026 with rising investor scrutiny. No write-down cycle had occurred by the cutoff.
verdictRationale: The arithmetic was transparent and the gap persists, but the predicted losses have not materialized or been ruled out. This is not falsified, and not vindicated either.
evolution: Later essays emphasise the physical buildout. A secondary source reports he raised the framing to ~$840B and later to a ~$3T revenue question with ~$1.5T infrastructure; not verified.
interpretations: Revenue grew far faster than skeptics expected (lab run-rates ~$65–70B by Sep 2026).
Annual capex (~$700B) still dwarfs revenue; the payback question remains open.

claim: The GPU shortage has subsided. GPU compute is becoming a commodity with weak pricing power, and new chips (B100) will accelerate depreciation of the existing H100 fleet.
assumptions: Supply catches up with demand
Each generation offers a large performance-per-dollar step
predictedOutcome: Falling GPU rental prices and faster depreciation of older accelerators. Compute providers lose pricing power.
contextAtTime: Mid-2024: H100 lead times had shortened and GPU rental prices were starting to fall.
outcome: Hyperscalers reported continued capacity constraints in 2026 (Wedbush on Alphabet: capacity 'remains constrained in the face of strong demand'), and memory costs rose. GPU-hour rental price declines in 2024–25 were not verified with a source during research.
verdictRationale: Commoditization of older GPU rentals likely occurred, but the 'shortage subsided' framing was contradicted by persistent 2025–26 capacity constraints as reasoning and agents drove inference demand.
evolution: Later essays turned to physical constraints (power, construction), which implies scarcity rather than glut.

claim: AI is now 'shovel ready': 2025 will be the 'Year of the Data Center', with a construction boom benefiting steel, energy (solar, batteries, nuclear) and construction, and operational challenges for hyperscalers.
assumptions: Hyperscalers follow through on capex commitments
Power and construction capacity become the critical path
predictedOutcome: A large, visible data-center construction boom in 2025, with execution and power challenges.
contextAtTime: 2024: capex guidance was rising but the physical buildout narrative was still emerging. The essay's publication date is uncertain.
outcome: 2025–2026 saw a historic data-center buildout: Stargate sites, ~7 GW planned by Sept 2025, and 2026 hyperscaler capex of ~$700B+. It came with delays, cancelled or reallocated expansions and power deals (SB Energy).
verdictRationale: The predicted boom and its physical bottlenecks materialized in 2025 as described.
evolution: Extended in later (unverified-date) Sequoia pieces noting data-center delays from power procurement and construction complexity.

claim: Speculative frenzies are a normal part of technology. Much value will be created by AI, but investors should not believe AGI-tomorrow 'get rich quick' delusions. Builders benefit as compute costs fall.
assumptions: Overbuild lowers compute costs for application builders
predictedOutcome: Some infrastructure investors lose money while application builders benefit from cheaper compute.
contextAtTime: Written in direct tension with AGI-timeline-driven investment theses such as Aschenbrenner's (same month).
outcome: Inference costs fell dramatically (ARK: >99% in a year by 2026), which helped builders. No broad infrastructure-investor losses had materialized by Oct 2026.
verdictRationale: The cost-decline leg is directionally supported. The loss leg is not yet tested.
evolution: No revision found.

claim: AI could replace roughly half of human jobs within about 10 years.
assumptions: Perception and decision AI automates routine cognitive and physical tasks quickly
Firms deploy rapidly
predictedOutcome: ~50% of jobs replaced (or replaceable) by ~2027.
contextAtTime: 2017: Frey & Osborne's 47% automation-risk estimate was widely cited. Deep-learning perception gains were fresh.
outcome: Through late 2025, studies found no broad labor-market disruption attributable to generative AI. The 2027 deadline has not passed.
verdictRationale: The deadline is 2027, but the trajectory is far off. 'Replace' is ambiguous between technical feasibility and actual displacement.
evolution: Restated in 2019 as ~40% within 15 years, which lengthened the horizon.

claim: The real threat of AI is not superintelligence but mass job loss and inequality. AI wealth will concentrate in a few US and Chinese companies, and other countries may have to strike deals with them.
assumptions: AI has winner-take-most economics
US and China dominate AI talent, data and capital
predictedOutcome: AI value concentrates in a small number of US/Chinese firms, and job displacement becomes the dominant policy issue.
contextAtTime: 2017: Musk and others emphasised existential risk. Lee was contrarian in prioritising labor and geopolitics.
outcome: AI value and investment concentrated heavily in US firms (OpenAI valued at $852B; four US hyperscalers spending ~$700B+ in 2026) and Chinese firms (DeepSeek, Alibaba). Mass job displacement had not materialized by late 2025.
verdictRationale: The concentration claim held strongly. The job-loss emphasis has not (yet) been borne out, and existential risk did not fade from the debate.
evolution: No revision found.

claim: Within about 15 years, AI could displace around 40% of the world's jobs.
assumptions: Steady diffusion of perception and decision AI into routine work
predictedOutcome: ~40% of global jobs displaced by ~2034.
contextAtTime: Pre-GPT-3, when automation-risk studies were commonly cited.
outcome: Not evaluable. No broad displacement had been measured by late 2025.
verdictRationale: The horizon is 2034.
evolution: Longer horizon than his 2017 '50% in 10 years' framing.

claim: China will match, and could overtake, the US in AI, because AI has entered an 'age of implementation' and 'age of data' that favour China's data abundance, entrepreneurs and state support.
assumptions: Data volume and implementation speed matter more than frontier research
China's consumer-internet scale translates into AI leadership
predictedOutcome: Chinese AI reaches parity with or leads the US.
contextAtTime: 2018: China led in computer vision deployment and mobile payments, while US firms dominated research.
outcome: By 2024–2026, Chinese models (DeepSeek, Qwen) reached near-parity on many benchmarks and led in open weights. The US still produced more notable models and dominated compute, capex and frontier revenue.
verdictRationale: Parity in model quality was largely achieved, but US leadership in compute, capital and frontier revenue persisted. China's catch-up was driven by engineering efficiency under compute constraints rather than data abundance.
evolution: By 2025 he emphasised that only a few Chinese giants can afford pretraining.

claim: The age of AI discovery is largely over. Deep learning was a rare breakthrough, and the next phase is implementation, where execution and data, not new research, determine winners.
assumptions: No new paradigm-level breakthroughs in the near term
predictedOutcome: Advantage shifts from research labs to implementers with data.
contextAtTime: The transformer (2017) existed, and GPT-1 and BERT appeared in 2018, but their significance was not yet widely appreciated.
outcome: The transformer/LLM scaling paradigm and reasoning RL (2018–2025) produced a new wave of discovery in which research and compute concentration were decisive. Lee himself founded an LLM lab in 2023.
verdictRationale: Judged on 2018 information, the claim was already contestable (transformers had been published). The subsequent LLM era was a discovery-driven paradigm shift.
evolution: Implicitly reversed by his 2023 'AI 2.0' framing and 01.AI's founding.

claim: Founded 01.AI to build world-class Chinese foundation models ('AI 2.0'), releasing the Yi series.
assumptions: A well-funded startup can sustain frontier pretraining in China despite export controls
predictedOutcome: Implied: 01.AI becomes a durable frontier-model developer.
contextAtTime: 2023: China's 'hundred-model war', with many startups raising funds to pretrain LLMs.
outcome: Yi-34B briefly led open leaderboards (late 2023). By early 2025 01.AI had stopped large-scale pretraining and pivoted to enterprise solutions on DeepSeek and other open models.
verdictRationale: The implied bet that 01.AI could remain a frontier pretrainer did not hold. This is an action, not a personal forecast, and the outcome evidence is Lee's own announcement.
evolution: Reversed in 2025 (pivot away from pretraining).

claim: Chinese labs can approach US frontier performance with a small fraction of the compute through engineering efficiency (e.g. Yi-Lightning reportedly trained for ~$3M on ~2,000 GPUs).
assumptions: Algorithmic and systems efficiency can offset export-controlled compute
predictedOutcome: Chinese near-frontier models trained at far lower cost than US counterparts.
contextAtTime: Late 2024: most Western observers assumed export controls would keep China well behind. DeepSeek-V3 arrived weeks later.
outcome: DeepSeek-V3 and R1 (Dec 2024–Jan 2025) delivered near-frontier performance with reported low training costs, and Chinese open-weight models became widely used.
verdictRationale: This was validated almost immediately by DeepSeek. Lee's own firm, however, was not the one to sustain it.
evolution: Led him to conclude in 2025 that only a few players need to pretrain, and that others should build on open models.

claim: 01.AI stops large-scale pretraining. China's foundation-model market will consolidate around DeepSeek, Alibaba and ByteDance.
assumptions: Pretraining costs keep rising
Open-weight leaders make second-tier pretraining uneconomic
predictedOutcome: Most Chinese LLM startups exit frontier pretraining, leaving ~3 dominant players.
contextAtTime: Shortly after DeepSeek-R1's success; China's 'AI tigers' were under funding pressure.
outcome: DeepSeek, Alibaba (Qwen) and ByteDance remained leading Chinese model developers. Some other labs (e.g. Moonshot, Zhipu, MiniMax) continued releasing competitive models; their 2026 status was not verified during research.
verdictRationale: The named three are leaders, but consolidation appears incomplete. The outcome evidence is thin and recalled.
evolution: No revision found.
